title: Run your first Python program
summary: Understand how source code becomes a result and distinguish printing from returning.
objectives: Run a short program and predict execution order
Distinguish source code, output, and error messages
Return a value from the provided solve function
lesson:
A Python program is a sequence of instructions written as text. An interpreter reads those instructions and carries them out. You can run Python in an interactive shell, a saved .py file, or a browser-based editor. In a terminal, a common command is python3 hello.py; some installations use python instead. A browser course environment may provide a Run button. The important idea is the same: editing text changes the recipe, while running it performs the recipe.

Think of execution as a bookmark moving down the program. In print("Ready"), the quoted text is a string value and print sends that value to the output area. Python does not print every value automatically in a script. The interactive shell sometimes displays expression results for convenience, which can make the two environments look different. Blank lines make code easier to read. A comment beginning with # explains intent and is not executed as an instruction.

Walk through the example one statement at a time. Python first creates a function called solve. Creating a function does not run its body. The later expression solve("Mina") calls that function with a name. Inside the function, "Hello, " + name + "!" joins three pieces of text. return hands the result back to the caller. Finally, print displays that returned result. The function therefore produces a reusable value rather than depending on a screen.

Course problems ask you to implement solve with a specific contract. Keep the requested function name and parameters. The test runner calls your function directly, so return the answer; do not replace return with print. A function that reaches its end without returning a value produces None, which is different from the expected string.

Common early mistakes are missing quotation marks, mismatched parentheses, and inconsistent indentation. Python uses indentation to group a function's body. Use four spaces and keep related statements aligned. When an error appears, first read the last line for the error type, then inspect the indicated source line. Start with the smallest working program, change one thing, and run it again. This edit-run-observe cycle is the foundation of every later debugging technique.

problems.title: A welcome label
problems.prompt: Implement solve(name). name is a string. Return "Welcome, " followed by name followed by "!". Preserve every character in name; an empty name is allowed. Do not print the answer.
problems.python:
def solve(name):
    return "Welcome, " + name + "!"
problems.explanation: The function receives a name that already exists as a Python string. There is no need to call input or to ask the user for it again. Build the answer by joining the fixed prefix, the supplied name, and the fixed suffix in that order. Spaces inside quotation marks are real characters, so the prefix includes exactly one space after the comma. The return statement sends the completed string to the test runner. Printing the string would display the right-looking text but would leave the function's return value as None. An empty name needs no special branch: joining an empty string adds zero characters. Testing that case checks that the punctuation belongs to the fixed pieces rather than to the name.
problems.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space, where n is the length of name.
hints: You need to produce one string value.
Use + to join the fixed text and the parameter.
Return "Welcome, " + name + "!".

quiz.question: What happens if the function only prints the label?
choices: The caller receives the printed string
quiz.explanation: Printing writes output; without an explicit return value, the function returns None.

problems.title: Echo with a divider
problems.prompt: Implement solve(text). Return two copies of the string text separated by exactly " | ". Keep original spacing and allow an empty string.
problems.python:
def solve(text):
    return text + " | " + text
problems.explanation: Separate the contract into three pieces: the first copy of text, the divider, and the second copy of text. Joining those pieces directly expresses the required output. The divider is a three-character string: a space, a vertical bar, and another space. The input string should be preserved exactly, so stripping whitespace or changing capitalization would break the contract even if the result looked neater. The empty-string case still includes the divider because the divider does not depend on the input having characters. This solution returns one value and has no side effects. Running the function with different inputs demonstrates that parameter values vary while the sequence of instructions stays the same. The returned string is newly constructed; the original input is unchanged.
problems.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space, where n is the length of text.
hints: Describe the answer as three adjacent pieces.
The middle piece is always " | ".
Use the text parameter on both sides of the divider.

quiz.question: For empty text, what should solve return?
quiz.explanation: Both copies contribute no characters, but the fixed divider remains.

title: Names, values, and types
summary: Use variables as names for values and recognize the basic data types.
objectives: Trace assignments and reassignment in order
Distinguish integers, floats, strings, and booleans
Build results using values without changing inputs
lesson:
A variable is a name that refers to a value. In tickets = 4, Python evaluates the right side and associates the resulting integer with the name tickets. The equals sign performs assignment; it does not state a permanent mathematical equality. If the next line is tickets = tickets + 2, Python reads the current value, computes six, and then reassigns the name. The old value is not an equation that must remain true.

A useful mental model is a label attached to a value. Moving a label does not retroactively change earlier calculations. Suppose original = 4 and doubled = original * 2. Reassigning original to 10 afterward leaves doubled equal to 8. Python follows execution order, rather than continuously recalculating dependent names as a spreadsheet might.

Values have types. An int represents an integer such as 7, a float represents a floating-point number such as 2.5, a str represents text such as "7", and a bool represents True or False. Quotation marks matter: 7 + 2 is numeric addition, while "7" + "2" joins text. Adding "7" to 2 raises a TypeError because Python will not silently choose between numeric addition and text construction. You can inspect a value's type with type(value) when exploring.

In the worked example, start refers to 8. The function stores start + gained in current, then subtracts spent. Each assignment has a clear purpose and the final return exposes only the answer. Calling solve does not change the integer held by the caller. Descriptive names make the sequence easier to inspect than names such as a, b, and c.

Common pitfalls include reading a name before assigning it, changing capitalization accidentally, and choosing names that hide built-in functions such as str or list. Python names are case-sensitive: score and Score are different names. Prefer lower_case_with_underscores and use names that express meaning. To check your understanding, write a tiny trace table on paper: after each line, record the names and their current values. Predict before running. If your prediction differs from the output, identify the first assignment where your mental model diverged.
python:
def solve(start, gained, spent):
    current = start + gained
    current = current - spent
    return current

print(solve(8, 5, 3))

problems.title: Track the balance
problems.prompt: Implement solve(start, gained, spent). All arguments are nonnegative integers. Return start + gained - spent. The result may be negative; do not clamp it to zero.
problems.python:
def solve(start, gained, spent):
    current = start + gained
    current = current - spent
    return current
problems.explanation: Begin with the starting balance and add the gained amount. Store that intermediate result in current so that its meaning remains visible during a walkthrough. Then subtract the spent amount and return the new balance. This mirrors the order described in the problem and provides two useful checkpoints while debugging. There is no requirement to reject an overspent balance, so a negative result is valid and must not be replaced with zero. The inputs are integers, and ordinary addition and subtraction keep the calculation exact. Assigning a new value to current does not change any caller-owned data. An equivalent one-expression solution is fine, but the intermediate name makes assignment and reassignment explicit for this lesson.
problems.complexity: O(1) arithmetic operations and O(1) auxiliary space under the standard integer model.
hints: Start from the supplied starting value.
Add gained before subtracting spent.
Return the result even when it is below zero.

quiz.question: After current = current - spent, what does current refer to?
quiz.explanation: The right side is evaluated first, and its result becomes the new value associated with current.

problems.title: A labeled score
problems.prompt: Implement solve(label, score). label is a string and score is an integer. Return label followed by ": " followed by the decimal representation of score. Preserve label exactly.
problems.explanation: The output is text, but one input is an integer. Convert that integer to a string with str before joining the pieces. This explicitly states the intended interpretation of the value instead of asking Python to guess what adding text and a number should mean. The label is already a string and should be copied exactly; the separator contributes the colon and one space. Negative integers naturally include a minus sign when converted, and zero becomes the single character "0". An empty label is still valid and leaves the separator at the beginning of the output. Keeping the conversion in a named intermediate variable makes the type change visible. Return the final string so callers can compare or reuse it.
problems.complexity: O(l + d) time and output space, where l is label length and d is the number of characters in str(score).
hints: The final result must contain only string pieces.
Convert score using str(score).
Join label, ": ", and the converted score.

quiz.question: Why is str(score) useful here?
choices: It changes the caller’s integer into text
It produces a string suitable for concatenation
quiz.explanation: str creates the text representation used in the returned label; it does not modify the caller’s value.

title: Arithmetic, division, and conversion
summary: Choose arithmetic operators by the meaning of the quantity you need.
objectives: Use // and % for complete groups and remainders
Convert valid numeric text into integers
Explain operator precedence and deliberate parentheses
lesson:
Arithmetic becomes easier when you identify the units and the question before choosing an operator. Addition combines quantities, subtraction measures a difference, and multiplication repeats a quantity. Division has two useful forms in Python: / produces a floating-point quotient, while // performs floor division. For nonnegative integers, floor division tells you how many complete groups fit. The remainder operator % tells you what is left after those groups are removed.

Imagine packing 17 counters into bags that hold 5. Three full bags use 15 counters, leaving 2. Python expresses these answers as 17 // 5 and 17 % 5. Together they satisfy total = groups * size + remainder. This relationship is a useful self-check. With nonnegative total and positive size, the remainder lies between zero and size minus one. Negative operands follow floor-division rules rather than truncation toward zero, so do not extend the packing picture to negatives without checking those rules.

The worked example converts a total number of seconds into minutes and leftover seconds. For 125 seconds, 125 // 60 gives 2 and 125 % 60 gives 5. Returning [minutes, seconds] keeps both results together in a small list. Lists are explored in detail later; here they are simply an ordered container whose first position means minutes.

Conversion is explicit. int("42") produces the integer 42 when the string is valid integer text. int("4.2") raises ValueError, because decimal-point text is not integer text. Converting a float with int truncates toward zero rather than rounding to the nearest integer. Use conversions because the input contract requires them, not as a way to hide an unexplained type mismatch.

Python applies multiplication and division before addition and subtraction. Parentheses make a different grouping explicit and can improve readability even when the default order is correct. Common mistakes include dividing by zero, using / when an integer count is needed, and confusing a remainder with a fractional quotient. For these exercises, trust the stated valid-input constraints. Test zero, an exact multiple, and a value just beyond a multiple; these three cases expose most beginner mistakes in grouping calculations.
python:
def solve(total_seconds):
    minutes = total_seconds // 60
    seconds = total_seconds % 60
    return [minutes, seconds]

print(solve(125))

problems.title: Full boxes and leftovers
problems.prompt: Implement solve(items, capacity). items is a nonnegative integer and capacity is a positive integer. Return [full_boxes, leftovers], counting only completely filled boxes.
problems.python:
def solve(items, capacity):
    return [items // capacity, items % capacity]
problems.explanation: Floor division counts how many complete groups of capacity can be formed from items. The remainder reports the number of items that do not belong to one of those complete groups. Return the two values in the requested order, because [leftovers, full_boxes] has different meaning even when it contains the same numbers. The capacity is guaranteed to be positive, so no zero-division branch is needed. If there are fewer items than the capacity, the full-box count is zero and all items remain. If items is exactly divisible, the remainder is zero. You can verify any answer by multiplying the first output by capacity and adding the second output; this should reconstruct the original item count.
problems.complexity: O(1) arithmetic operations and O(1) auxiliary space under the standard integer model.
hints: One operator counts complete groups.
Use // for full boxes and % for leftovers.
Return the quotient first and the remainder second.

quiz.question: Which relation should always hold?
quiz.explanation: Each full box accounts for capacity items; the remainder accounts for everything else.

problems.title: Add integer text
problems.prompt: Implement solve(left, right). Both strings contain valid base-10 integers, optionally with surrounding whitespace and a leading + or - sign. Return their numeric sum as an integer.
problems.python:
def solve(left, right):
    left_value = int(left)
    right_value = int(right)
    return left_value + right_value
problems.explanation: The arguments arrive as text, but the contract asks for a numeric sum. Parse each argument with int to obtain integer values, then add those values. Adding the original strings would concatenate their characters and would not implement arithmetic. Python's int conversion accepts surrounding whitespace and an optional leading sign for these valid inputs, so separate trimming or sign-handling code is unnecessary. Return the resulting integer directly rather than converting it back to text. The output type is part of the contract just as much as the output value. The problem guarantees valid integer strings, so an exception handler for invalid text would add an unrequested behavior. The zero and mixed-sign tests confirm both parsing and actual numeric addition.
problems.complexity: O(a + b) input scanning for a- and b-character strings, plus integer arithmetic cost; storage includes the parsed integers.
hints: Determine the type the answer should have.
Convert both strings before adding them.
Use int(left) + int(right), not left + right.

quiz.question: What does "12" + "5" evaluate to?
quiz.explanation: The + operator concatenates two strings; numeric addition requires conversion first.

title: Make decisions with conditions
summary: Translate precise rules into mutually exclusive branches.
objectives: Evaluate comparisons and Boolean combinations
Use if, elif, and else in a deliberate order
Test both sides of every boundary
lesson:
A condition is an expression whose truth determines which instructions run. Comparisons such as score >= 60 or count == 0 produce Boolean values. Notice that == compares two values, while = assigns a value to a name. An if statement evaluates its condition and runs its indented body only when the condition is true. An optional else body runs when that condition is false.

Think of an if/elif/else chain as a sequence of gates. Python tests the first gate, then moves to the next only if the earlier one did not open. Once a branch is selected, the remaining branches in that chain are skipped. Separate if statements behave differently: more than one can run. Choose a chain when the contract calls for exactly one category.

In the example, temperatures below zero are "freezing", values from zero through nineteen are "cool", and all larger values are "warm". A value of -3 selects the first branch. A value of 12 fails the first condition and succeeds at the second. There is no need to repeat temperature >= 0 in the second condition, because reaching it already proves the first condition was false. A value of 20 reaches the final return.

The operators and, or, and not combine or reverse conditions. For example, age >= 18 and has_ticket requires both facts to be true. Write each comparison in full: value == 1 or value == 2 is different from value == 1 or 2. The latter contains the standalone truthy number 2 and therefore does not express the intended comparison.

Most conditional bugs occur at boundaries or in branch ordering. A broad condition placed first can make a narrower later branch unreachable. Equality deserves explicit attention: does the cutoff belong to the lower group or the upper group? Before coding, write one example below a cutoff, one exactly on it, and one above it. Trace which branch each should take. Resist adding unstated categories or validation rules. A correct program implements the stated contract, including its precise labels, capitalization, and boundary behavior.

problems.title: Compare with a target
problems.prompt: Implement solve(value, target) for two integers. Return "below" when value < target, "equal" when they match, and "above" otherwise.
problems.explanation: There are exactly three possible relationships between the integers: smaller, equal, or larger. Check the smaller case first and return its label immediately. If execution continues, that case is already excluded. Check equality next, again returning immediately when it holds. Reaching the final statement means that neither smaller nor equal was true, so the value must be larger. This uses early returns to express the same mutually exclusive logic as an if/elif/else chain. The exact output labels matter, including lowercase spelling. Negative values need no special treatment because integer comparisons already order them correctly. Testing equal inputs is especially important because a solution that checks only smaller versus everything else would incorrectly classify the boundary.
problems.complexity: O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space under the standard integer model.
hints: Write down all three possible relationships.
Handle equality explicitly.
After excluding below and equal, return above.

quiz.question: If value and target are equal, is value < target true?
quiz.explanation: Strict less-than excludes equality, so equality needs its own branch.

problems.title: Shipping-band label
problems.prompt: Implement solve(weight). weight is a nonnegative integer. Return "letter" for weights 0 through 100, "parcel" for weights 101 through 1000, and "freight" for weights above 1000.
problems.explanation: Check the smallest upper boundary first. If weight is at most 100, the answer is letter and the function can return immediately. Otherwise, execution has established that weight is greater than 100. The next comparison therefore only needs to check the upper boundary of the parcel range. If that comparison also fails, the weight is above 1000 and belongs to freight. Ordering these tests from the smallest threshold to the largest keeps the logic compact and avoids repeating facts already known from the control flow. Both cutoffs are inclusive, so <= is required rather than <. The tests include exact boundaries and the first value of the next band, which helps reveal off-by-one mistakes that ordinary middle-of-range examples would miss.
problems.complexity: O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Start with the smallest category.
Both 100 and 1000 belong to the category ending at that number.
Use <= 100, then <= 1000, then the final category.

quiz.question: Why can the second branch omit weight > 100?
choices: Reaching it means the first condition failed
quiz.explanation: The first branch already handled every weight at or below 100.

title: Repeat work with loops
summary: Use iteration and accumulators without losing track of state.
objectives: Trace a for loop over a range
Maintain a running total or count
Explain why empty iterations need a valid initial result
lesson:
A loop repeats a block of instructions. A for loop visits each item in an iterable, assigning that item to the loop variable before running the body. For beginner counting tasks, range supplies a sequence of integers without requiring you to write them out. range(4) visits 0, 1, 2, and 3. Its stopping value is excluded. range(1, 5) visits 1 through 4.

A useful mental model is a worker moving across a row of cards. The loop variable holds the current card, while other variables record accumulated information about the cards already processed. These roles are different. In a sum, number identifies the current item and total remembers the running answer. Initialize total before entering the loop so it survives from one iteration to the next.

The example adds the integers from one through n. For n = 3, total begins at zero. The first iteration adds 1, producing 1. The second adds 2, producing 3. The third adds 3, producing 6. The function returns only after all three iterations finish. For n = 0, range(1, 1) is empty and the body never runs, leaving total at the correct answer of zero.

A while loop repeats while a condition remains true. It is helpful when the number of repetitions is not known in advance, but the body must move the state toward termination. Forgetting that progress can create an infinite loop. Prefer a for loop when you already know the values you need to visit.

Common pitfalls include excluding the desired last value, resetting the accumulator inside the loop, and placing return inside the body by accident. An early return stops the whole function, not just the current iteration. To debug, trace a tiny example with columns for the current item and the accumulated value after processing it. Include an empty case and a one-item case. These reveal whether initialization, loop boundaries, and the final return each have the correct role. Once you understand the loop, you can later compare it with a formula or a built-in operation.

problems.title: Add through the endpoint
problems.prompt: Implement solve(n). n is an integer from 0 through 10000. Return the sum of all integers from 1 through n, inclusive. Practice using a loop and accumulator.
problems.explanation: Initialize the total to zero because no values have been processed yet. Visit each integer beginning at one and ending at n. Since range excludes its stop argument, use n + 1 as that argument to include n itself. Add each visited value to the running total and return only after the loop completes. The variable total then represents the sum of all values processed so far, which is a simple loop invariant. For n equal to zero, there are no values to add and the initial zero is already correct. A closed-form formula also exists, but the loop is valuable here because it exposes initialization, repeated state updates, and termination as separate steps you can trace.
problems.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Begin with the sum of zero processed numbers.
range stops before its second argument.
Use range(1, n + 1) and add each value to total.

quiz.question: Where should total = 0 appear?
quiz.explanation: The accumulator must be initialized once and retain its updated value between iterations.

problems.title: Count divisible values
problems.prompt: Implement solve(limit, divisor). limit is an integer from 0 through 10000 and divisor is a positive integer. Return how many integers from 1 through limit, inclusive, are divisible by divisor. Practice checking values in a loop.
problems.explanation: Visit every integer in the specified inclusive range. A value is divisible by divisor exactly when its remainder after division is zero. When that condition holds, add one to the count; otherwise leave the count unchanged. The accumulator tracks qualifying values, not the sum of those values, so the update is count += 1 rather than count += value. Initialize count before the loop and return after it. An empty range naturally produces zero because no successful checks occur. When divisor is larger than limit, no positive value in the range qualifies. Although integer division can compute the same answer directly, this implementation intentionally practices combining a loop with a condition, a pattern that will remain useful when no simple formula exists.
problems.complexity: O(limit) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Check each candidate in the requested interval.
Divisibility means a remainder of zero.
Increment count by one only when value % divisor == 0.

quiz.question: What should the accumulator add when a value qualifies?
quiz.explanation: This is a counting problem: each qualifying value contributes one to the answer.

title: Nested loops and invariants
summary: Reason about repeated work inside repeated work and prove what accumulators mean.
objectives: Trace outer and inner loop iterations
State a simple loop invariant in ordinary language
Estimate the work in a rectangular pair search
lesson:
A nested loop places one loop inside another. For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs through its own sequence. If the outer loop visits three rows and the inner loop visits four columns, the body runs twelve times. The inner loop restarts for every row; it does not resume where the previous row ended.

Picture a grid. The outer variable selects a row and the inner variable selects a column. Together they identify one position. This mental model helps with coordinate generation, pair comparisons, and small exhaustive searches. It also explains why two loops can be more expensive than one: a rectangle with r rows and c columns contains r times c positions.

The worked example counts pairs whose sum is even. For a = 2 and b = 3, the candidate pairs are (1,1), (1,2), (1,3), (2,1), (2,2), and (2,3). Exactly three have even sums. The count begins at zero and increases only for a qualifying pair. The loops enumerate each candidate once, so no valid pair is skipped or double-counted.

An invariant is a statement that remains true at a chosen point during repeated execution. Here, after each inner-body execution, count equals the number of qualifying pairs already visited. Before any pair, the count is zero, so the statement holds initially. Each update preserves it. When all pairs have been visited, that same statement establishes the answer. You do not need formal notation to use invariants; a precise sentence can guide both implementation and debugging.

Pay attention to which state belongs to the whole computation and which belongs to a single row. A grand total should be initialized outside both loops. A per-row subtotal should be initialized inside the outer loop but before the inner loop. Mixing those positions produces plausible but wrong results. Common pitfalls also include accidentally using the outer limit for both ranges and assuming an empty dimension still creates pairs. If either dimension is zero, there are no grid positions. Test unequal dimensions, a one-by-one grid, and an empty dimension before trusting a nested-loop solution.

problems.title: Grid coordinate labels
problems.prompt: Implement solve(rows, columns). Both are integers from 0 through 30. Return a list of [row, column] pairs for every grid position, using zero-based coordinates and row-major order: all columns of row 0 first, then row 1, and so on.
problems.explanation: Create an empty result list before either loop. The outer loop chooses each row in increasing order, while the inner loop chooses each column for that row. Append a fresh two-element list for every visited position. This loop ordering directly produces row-major order without a later sort. The result contains exactly the positions visited so far, which provides an invariant for checking the algorithm. Zero-based ranges are convenient because range(rows) and range(columns) already start at zero and exclude their upper bounds. If either dimension is zero, no positions are appended and the answer is empty. The output is intentionally a list of lists so it remains compatible with the exercise's JSON test format and preserves the requested sequence.
problems.complexity: O(rows × columns + rows) time for this loop structure; O(rows × columns) output space and O(1) auxiliary space besides output.
hints: Choose a row before choosing its columns.
Use one loop for rows and an inner loop for columns.
Append [row, column] to one result list inside the inner loop.

quiz.question: Which loop belongs on the outside for row-major order?
quiz.explanation: Finishing all inner columns before moving the outer row produces row-major order.

problems.title: Target-sum pairs
problems.prompt: Implement solve(a, b, target). a and b are integers from 0 through 100; target is any integer. Count ordered pairs (x, y) where 1 <= x <= a, 1 <= y <= b, and x + y == target. Return the count.
problems.explanation: Enumerate the entire rectangle of legal pairs using one loop for x and one for y. Each combination appears exactly once, so it is safe to increment a count whenever its sum matches the target. For the sample, the successful pairs are (1,4), (2,3), and (3,2). Ordered pairs distinguish the first coordinate's role from the second, and the two coordinates have separate upper bounds. Keep the count outside both loops because it summarizes all visited pairs, not just one row. Empty coordinate ranges produce no pairs. The small input limits make exhaustive enumeration appropriate for this lesson. Later, the equation y = target - x allows an O(a) method, but the direct search is easier to verify and establishes the baseline reasoning.
problems.complexity: O(a × b + a) time for the nested loops and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Generate each legal value of x and each legal value of y.
Check the sum inside the inner loop.
Keep one counter outside both loops and increment it only on equality.

quiz.question: What should count represent after each candidate is checked?
choices: All pairs in the full grid
Matching pairs among candidates already visited
quiz.explanation: That invariant is initially true and is preserved by each conditional increment.

title: Function contracts, parameters, and scope
summary: Turn a calculation into a reusable function with a clear boundary.
objectives: Distinguish a parameter from an argument
Return a result on every required execution path
Keep temporary names local to a function
lesson:
A function packages instructions behind a name. Its parameters describe the information it needs, and its return value describes the information it produces. In def double(value), value is a parameter. In double(7), the supplied 7 is an argument. Each call binds the parameters to that call's arguments and then executes the body.

Think of a function as a small workshop with an intake and an output hatch. Its contract says what kinds of inputs are accepted, what answer is returned, and whether anything outside the workshop changes. A good contract removes guesswork. For example, a function that divides a bill needs to say whether a zero-person input is allowed and whether the answer is an integer or a decimal. These choices should come from the problem statement, not from assumptions hidden in the code.

The worked example computes a rectangle's perimeter. width and height receive the caller's values. The intermediate name half_perimeter exists locally inside the call. return sends the doubled value back to the caller and immediately ends that function call. The caller stores the result in answer and can then print it, compare it, or pass it elsewhere. Keeping printing outside the calculation makes the function easier to test and reuse.

A local variable is normally accessible only within its function. Two functions can each use a name such as total without sharing that variable. Avoid depending on global state for these exercises. A function whose output depends only on its explicit inputs is easier to reason about because a test can fully describe its situation.

Watch for missing returns. If one branch returns an answer but another reaches the end, the latter returns None. Also remember that code after an unconditional return in the same path never executes. Reassigning a parameter name is a local operation; changing the contents of a mutable object such as a list can affect the caller, which we will revisit in the collections lessons. For now, keep the requested signature unchanged, use meaningful local names, and check every possible path against the output contract. Small, explicit functions become building blocks for larger programs.
python:
def solve(width, height):
    half_perimeter = width + height
    return 2 * half_perimeter

answer = solve(3, 5)
print(answer)

problems.title: Rectangle perimeter
problems.prompt: Implement solve(width, height). Both arguments are nonnegative integers. Return the rectangle perimeter 2 * (width + height). Zero dimensions are allowed and use the same formula.
problems.explanation: The contract provides both dimensions directly, so the function should not read extra input or depend on an outside variable. Add width and height to obtain the length of two adjacent sides. A rectangle has two copies of each dimension, so doubling that sum gives its perimeter. The local name half_perimeter records the meaning of the intermediate calculation and exists only during this call. Return the numeric answer rather than printing it. Parentheses or the intermediate assignment ensure that both dimensions are doubled, avoiding the different expression 2 * width + height. The problem explicitly allows zero dimensions, so those inputs still use the formula instead of raising an error or inventing a special label. Every path returns an integer.
problems.complexity: O(1) arithmetic operations and O(1) auxiliary space under the standard integer model.
hints: A rectangle has two widths and two heights.
Group width + height before doubling it.
Return 2 * (width + height).

quiz.question: What does a local intermediate name improve?
choices: It explains the value’s role without changing the contract
It shares data across all functions
It replaces the need for return
quiz.explanation: A meaningful local name clarifies the calculation while remaining internal to the function.

problems.title: Clamp to a permitted interval
problems.prompt: Implement solve(value, lower, upper). All inputs are integers and lower <= upper. Return lower if value is below the interval, upper if it is above the interval, and value otherwise. Do not change the bounds.
problems.explanation: Check whether the value is too small and return the lower boundary if it is. If it is not too small, check whether it is too large and return the upper boundary when necessary. A value that passes both checks lies inside the inclusive interval and should be returned unchanged. The final return is essential: leaving it out would produce None for the most ordinary inputs. Values exactly equal to either boundary are already valid. When lower equals upper, every input is mapped to that one permitted value through the same logic. The function depends only on its explicit arguments and has no external side effects. This makes each test a complete description of a call and keeps the behavior consistent across repeated calls.
problems.complexity: O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Identify below, above, and inside as three cases.
Each out-of-range case returns its nearest bound.
After both strict comparisons fail, return value.

quiz.question: What happens if the final return value is omitted?
quiz.explanation: When neither conditional branch returns, the function falls through and returns None.

title: Read errors and debug deliberately
summary: Use evidence to locate failures instead of changing code at random.
objectives: Distinguish syntax errors, runtime exceptions, and wrong answers
Read a traceback from the final error back to relevant code
Use a minimal failing example to test a hypothesis
lesson:
Debugging means finding the gap between intended behavior and actual behavior. Three broad failure categories help you choose a starting point. A syntax error means Python cannot parse the program, perhaps because a colon or closing parenthesis is missing. A runtime exception happens while valid code executes, such as dividing by zero or accessing a nonexistent list position. A logic error produces a result that does not match the contract without necessarily raising an exception.

Treat debugging as a small experiment. First state the expected result for one concrete input. Then run the code and record what actually happens. Form one hypothesis about the difference, make the smallest relevant change, and run the same input again. Changing several unrelated lines at once makes it harder to know which change helped and which introduced a new problem.

Read a traceback from its final line to learn the exception type and message, then inspect the referenced line in your own code. A TypeError often indicates an operation used incompatible types. A NameError may indicate a misspelled or unassigned name. An IndexError often indicates an invalid position. These are clues, not instructions to suppress the exception. Catching every error and returning a default answer can conceal the real bug.

The example converts total minutes into hours and leftover minutes. A flawed version might use / for hours and accidentally return a float, or subtract hours rather than hours * 60 when computing the remainder. Test 125 minutes: the expected answer is [2, 5]. Inspecting hours and remainder separately exposes which step is wrong. The corrected version uses quotient and remainder directly.

Temporary print statements can reveal intermediate values when exploring locally, but remove noisy diagnostics from a final solution. Assertions can express expectations during development, though they should not substitute for the specified input contract. Common debugging mistakes include fixing only the sample, adding unexplained special cases, and ignoring the smallest failing input. After a fix, rerun old passing cases too. A successful repair explains why the original failure occurred and why the corrected logic works for the entire allowed input range.
python:
def solve(total_minutes):
    hours = total_minutes // 60
    minutes = total_minutes % 60
    return [hours, minutes]

print(solve(125))

problems.title: Repair an inclusive sum
problems.prompt: Implement solve(n) for integers 0 through 10000. Return 1 + 2 + ... + n, or 0 when n is 0. A previous version used range(1, n), incorrectly omitting the endpoint. Write the corrected loop.
problems.explanation: The reported bug is a mismatch between the inclusive mathematical interval and Python's exclusive range stop. The range must stop at n + 1 so that n is visited. Keep the accumulator initialized to zero and return it after the loop, since those parts already match the intended behavior. A useful minimal failing case for the original bug is n equal to one: range(1, 1) is empty and incorrectly gives zero. After the repair, that case gives one. The empty case n equal to zero still works because range(1, 1) performs no iterations. Rerunning both small and larger cases confirms that the change fixes the boundary rule rather than simply patching the sample output.
problems.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Find the difference between an inclusive endpoint and range’s stop.
The last value visited by range(1, stop) is stop - 1.
Set the stop to n + 1.

quiz.question: Which input is a minimal positive counterexample to range(1, n)?
quiz.explanation: For n = 1, the original range is empty, but the required sum is one.

problems.title: Repair ceiling division
problems.prompt: Implement solve(tasks, batch_size). tasks is a nonnegative integer and batch_size is a positive integer. Return the minimum number of batches needed when each batch holds at most batch_size tasks. A previous version always added 1 to tasks // batch_size; fix exact multiples and zero.
problems.explanation: Floor division counts the completely filled batches. An extra batch is required only when some tasks remain after those complete batches. Check that remainder explicitly instead of always adding one. For ten tasks with a batch size of four, two full batches cover eight tasks and the remainder of two requires a third batch. For eight tasks with the same capacity, the remainder is zero and two batches are sufficient. Zero tasks also produce zero complete batches and zero remainder, so no special case is needed. This repair follows the reason the previous code failed: it treated an empty remainder as though unfinished work remained. Testing below, exactly on, and just above a multiple verifies the corrected boundary behavior.
problems.complexity: O(1) arithmetic operations and O(1) auxiliary space under the standard integer model.
hints: Full batches and leftover tasks are different quantities.
Only a nonzero remainder needs another batch.
Start with tasks // batch_size, then conditionally add one.

quiz.question: When is the extra batch necessary?
choices: Only when tasks % batch_size is nonzero
quiz.explanation: A nonzero remainder represents tasks that have not yet been assigned to a complete batch.

title: Design tests around boundaries
summary: Use examples, edge cases, and properties to challenge your own solution.
objectives: Derive expected answers independently of the implementation
Select empty, singleton, boundary, and ordinary cases
Use properties to check families of outputs
lesson:
A test combines inputs with an expected result. It is useful only when that expected result is trustworthy. Derive small answers by hand before running your implementation, rather than copying the program's output into a test. Otherwise, the test may simply preserve the same mistake. A sample demonstrates one behavior; it does not prove all permitted inputs are handled.

Think of test design as asking targeted questions. An ordinary case asks whether the main idea works. A boundary case asks which side of a cutoff includes equality. An empty case asks whether initialization is sensible when no work occurs. A singleton case asks whether the smallest nonempty situation is handled. A repeated-value case asks whether you accidentally assumed uniqueness.

The worked example checks whether a value lies inside an inclusive interval. A strong small suite includes a value below the lower bound, exactly at the lower bound, inside, exactly at the upper bound, and above it. It also includes a collapsed interval whose lower and upper bounds are equal. These examples are chosen because they distinguish correct comparisons from plausible alternatives such as strict inequalities.

Properties can complement individual examples. A clamping function should always return a value between its bounds. Applying it twice should produce the same result as applying it once. A sorting function should preserve the number of elements and their multiplicities. Properties do not replace exact-output tests, because a wrong constant answer might satisfy a weak property, but they can expose failures across many inputs.

Use assert during local practice to compare an actual result with an expected one. A failing assertion should send you back to a specific input and contract, not immediately to a guessed code change. Common pitfalls include ignoring the output type, testing only positive numbers when negatives are allowed, and using random tests without a reliable way to compute the answer. For mutable inputs, remember that one test should not corrupt the starting data for another. Keep cases independent, choose small counterexamples that reveal the fault clearly, and retain every discovered regression case so the same bug is harder to reintroduce.
python:
def solve(value, lower, upper):
    return lower <= value <= upper

assert solve(3, 3, 8) is True
assert solve(9, 3, 8) is False
assert solve(4, 4, 4) is True
print("Checks passed")

problems.title: Inclusive interval membership
problems.prompt: Implement solve(value, lower, upper). Inputs are integers with lower <= upper. Return a Boolean indicating whether lower <= value <= upper. Both endpoints are included.
problems.python:
def solve(value, lower, upper):
    return lower <= value <= upper
problems.explanation: A value belongs to the interval when it satisfies both the lower and upper constraints. Python's chained comparison expresses these constraints directly and returns a Boolean. Equality is allowed at each end, so both comparison operators must include the equals sign. Do not return the strings "True" or "False" because the contract requires Boolean values. To test the logic, choose values on each boundary and immediately outside the interval, then check an ordinary inside value. A collapsed interval deserves attention: when lower and upper are identical, exactly that one value is accepted. These tests distinguish inclusive membership from strict membership and from accidentally checking only one boundary. They also demonstrate that test selection should follow the contract's decision points.
problems.complexity: O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: Both lower and upper conditions must hold.
Equality is accepted at either endpoint.
Return lower <= value <= upper.

quiz.question: Which test specifically checks the lower endpoint’s inclusion?
quiz.explanation: A value exactly equal to the lower bound distinguishes <= from < at that boundary.

problems.title: Count sign changes
problems.prompt: Implement solve(values). values is a list of integers. Remove zeros conceptually, then count how often consecutive remaining values have opposite signs. Return 0 when fewer than two nonzero values remain. Do not modify values.
problems.explanation: Track the sign of the previous nonzero value rather than the previous list position. Zero values are skipped and must not reset that remembered sign, because the contract removes them conceptually. Use zero as an initial sentinel meaning that no nonzero value has been seen yet. For each nonzero input, compute either positive sign one or negative sign minus one. If a previous sign exists and differs from the current sign, increment the change count. Then remember the current sign for the next comparison. Empty and all-zero inputs never create a comparison, and a singleton nonzero input establishes a sign without creating a change. The scan reads the list without deleting items, so it preserves caller data and avoids index-shifting bugs.
problems.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for n input values.
hints: Zeros do not separate the remaining sequence.
Remember only the previous nonzero sign.
Skip zero, compare signs when a previous one exists, then update the remembered sign.

quiz.question: What should a zero do to the remembered nonzero sign?
quiz.explanation: Zeros are conceptually removed, so the comparison must bridge across them.

title: Lists, tuples, and safe iteration
summary: Work with ordered collections while distinguishing copying from shared mutation.
objectives: Index and slice lists while respecting their boundaries
Distinguish aliases, shallow copies, and immutable tuples
Use enumerate and simple comprehensions readably
lesson:
A list is an ordered, mutable collection. In scores = [7, 4, 9], scores[0] is 7 because indexing starts at zero. scores[-1] accesses the last element. A tuple such as (7, 4) is also ordered, but its element references cannot be reassigned. Tuples work well for fixed records; lists work well for sequences that grow or change. An empty collection has length zero and no valid element index.

Think of a list as a shared row of slots. Assigning alias = scores creates another name for the same list, not another row. Changing alias[0] also changes scores[0]. In contrast, copied = scores[:] makes a shallow copy: the outer list is new, though nested mutable elements remain shared. A slice scores[start:stop] includes start and excludes stop. scores[1:] copies everything after the first element. Unlike direct indexing, a slice can safely extend beyond a list's end.

Iterate directly with for score in scores when you only need values. Use enumerate(scores) when you need each index and value together; it yields pairs that can be unpacked as index, score. Use range(len(scores)) when an index-driven algorithm genuinely needs positions, rather than as an automatic replacement for direct iteration. Avoid deleting elements from a list while iterating over that same list, because shifting positions can cause skipped values.

The worked example first demonstrates that assigning alias shares mutation, while a slice preserves the earlier outer-list values. It then uses enumerate to pair positions with values. Finally, the comprehension [score * 2 for score in scores] builds a new list by transforming each value. A comprehension is a compact spelling of a simple loop that appends results. Keep it readable; complicated branches or multiple responsibilities usually belong in an ordinary loop.

Common mistakes include accessing index len(scores), forgetting that slices exclude their stop, and assuming a shallow copy recursively duplicates nested lists. For these exercises, do not mutate the input unless the contract explicitly requests it. Building a fresh output list is often the clearest approach. Test an empty list, a one-element list, repeated values, and a case where output order matters.
python:
scores = [7, 4, 9]
alias = scores
copied = scores[:]
alias[0] = 8
print(scores, copied)
print([[index, score] for index, score in enumerate(scores)])
doubled = [score * 2 for score in scores]
print(doubled)

problems.title: Double a fresh list
problems.prompt: Implement solve(values). values is a list of integers. Return a new list containing twice each input value in the same order. Do not modify values. Practice a simple list comprehension.
problems.python:
def solve(values):
    return [value * 2 for value in values]
problems.explanation: A list comprehension creates a new list by evaluating its leading expression once for each value in the source sequence. Here, that expression doubles the current integer, so the result has the same length and order as the input. Because the comprehension builds a separate outer list, it does not assign into any input position or mutate the caller's collection. Negative integers and zero obey the same multiplication rule and need no branches. An empty input produces an empty result because there are no iterations. The equivalent ordinary loop would create result = [], append value * 2 for each item, and return result. Understanding that expansion makes comprehensions easier to read and helps you reserve them for simple transformations.
problems.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space; O(1) auxiliary space besides the output.
hints: Transform each value independently.
The output expression is value * 2.
Build [value * 2 for value in values].

quiz.question: Does assigning doubled = values create an independent list?
choices: No, it creates another reference to the same list
Only if the list is empty
quiz.explanation: Assignment aliases the list; a comprehension constructs a fresh list.

problems.title: Positions above the cutoff
problems.prompt: Implement solve(values, cutoff). values is a list of integers and cutoff is an integer. Return the zero-based indices whose values are strictly greater than cutoff, in increasing index order. Do not modify values.
problems.explanation: The problem asks for positions, not the qualifying values themselves. enumerate supplies each zero-based index together with its value, keeping those two roles explicit. Compare the value with cutoff and append the corresponding index only when the comparison is strictly true. Visiting the list from left to right automatically places result indices in increasing order. Repeated qualifying values may appear at different positions, and each position must be included separately. A value exactly equal to cutoff does not qualify. The loop reads the original list and appends to a separate result list, so the input remains unchanged. Empty input returns an empty result, and an input with no qualifying values does the same for a different reason.
problems.complexity: O(n) time and O(k) output space for k qualifying indices; O(1) auxiliary space besides output.
hints: You need both each value and its position.
enumerate(values) supplies index and value together.
Append index when value > cutoff, not when value >= cutoff.

quiz.question: What should be appended for a qualifying element?
quiz.explanation: The requested output is a list of zero-based positions, so append index.

title: Dictionaries, sets, and membership
summary: Choose a keyed collection for lookup, counting, or uniqueness.
objectives: Use dictionary keys and get for frequency counts
Use sets to track whether a value has appeared
Preserve required order separately from membership state
lesson:
A dictionary maps keys to values. For example, counts = {"red": 2, "blue": 1} associates each color with its frequency. A set stores distinct values and answers membership questions without associating a separate value with each member. Use a dictionary when you need information per key; use a set when you only need to know whether a value is present.

Think of a dictionary as labeled drawers and a set as a guest list. The expression key in counts checks dictionary keys, not dictionary values. Reading counts[key] raises KeyError if the key does not exist. counts.get(key, 0) instead returns zero for an absent key without inserting it. The assignment counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0) + 1 both creates a first count and increments later counts.

The worked example counts words one at a time. On the first "sun", get returns zero and the stored value becomes one. "rain" creates another key. The next "sun" changes only its own count to two. The dictionary now summarizes the processed prefix of the input. Keys must be hashable; strings and integers work well, while lists cannot be dictionary keys or set elements. These exercises use simple JSON-compatible string values.

Set membership supports a different pattern: record what you have already seen. If word is not in seen, it is a first occurrence; you can append it to an output list and add it to seen. Do not rely on iterating a set to reproduce input order. If order matters, preserve it explicitly in a list. A dictionary preserves insertion order in modern Python, but a set does not promise a useful sequence order.

Common pitfalls include assuming a dictionary lookup checks values, treating missing keys as automatically zero, and using a set when duplicate counts are important. Membership and updates in dictionaries and sets are expected constant-time operations under ordinary hashing assumptions, rather than a guarantee for every possible case. Test repeated values, empty inputs, and different capitalization. Unless the contract requests normalization, "Sun" and "sun" are different strings. Choose the collection that matches the question, and keep output requirements separate from your internal storage choice.

problems.title: Word frequencies
problems.prompt: Implement solve(words). words is a list of strings. Return a dictionary mapping each distinct string to its occurrence count. Matching is case-sensitive, empty strings are valid keys, and input order does not affect dictionary equality. Do not modify words.
problems.explanation: Create an empty dictionary and process each word once. For the current word, retrieve its existing count with a default of zero, then store one more than that count. The same update handles first appearances and repeats, so no separate branch is required. After each iteration, the dictionary contains exact frequencies for the processed part of the list. At the end, that invariant describes the entire input. Matching is deliberately case-sensitive, so do not lowercase words or strip their whitespace. An empty string is a valid dictionary key and should be counted like any other string. Empty input leaves the dictionary empty. The input list is only read, and the returned dictionary is a new collection owned by the result.
problems.complexity: Expected O(n) dictionary operations and O(u) output entries for n words and u distinct words; string hashing cost also depends on word lengths.
hints: Store one count per distinct word.
Use get(word, 0) for words not yet present.
Assign counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1 on every visit.

quiz.question: What does counts.get(word, 0) do when word is absent?
choices: Returns zero without inserting the key
quiz.explanation: get supplies a fallback value; the later assignment performs the actual insertion.

problems.title: Keep first occurrences
problems.prompt: Implement solve(words). words is a list of strings. Return a list containing each distinct string exactly once, ordered by its first appearance. Matching is case-sensitive. Do not modify words.
problems.explanation: Use two collections with different responsibilities. The set seen answers whether a word has appeared before, while result preserves the order in which first appearances were encountered. Scan the input from left to right. When a word is absent from seen, append it to result and add it to the set. When it is already present, skip it. Appending only on the first visit guarantees uniqueness, and the scan order guarantees the required first-appearance ordering. Returning list(set(words)) would remove duplicates but would not establish the requested order. Empty strings and capitalization differences follow ordinary string equality without extra normalization. The original list remains unchanged because all additions are made to newly created collections.
problems.complexity: Expected O(n) set operations and O(u) auxiliary/output entries for u distinct words; string hashing cost depends on word lengths.
hints: You need fast membership checks and preserved output order.
Use a set for membership and a list for the answer.
Append and mark a word only the first time it is encountered.

quiz.question: Why not simply return list(set(words))?
choices: It may fail to preserve first-appearance order
Lists cannot be built from sets
quiz.explanation: A set tracks membership, but its iteration order is not the input’s first-occurrence order.

title: Strings as immutable sequences
summary: Transform text carefully with indexing, slicing, splitting, and joining.
objectives: Explain why string operations create new values
Use split and join to process whitespace-separated words
Normalize text only when the contract asks for it
lesson:
A string is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters. You can inspect its length, visit its characters, index it, and take slices, much as with a list. However, text[0] = "A" is not allowed: individual positions in a string cannot be reassigned. Operations such as text.lower() or text.strip() produce new strings rather than changing the original one.

Think of text processing as a pipeline of transformations. Decide what each stage means and which details it is allowed to discard. strip removes whitespace from the ends, lower changes letter case, and split separates text into pieces. Calling split() without an argument treats runs of whitespace as separators and omits empty pieces. Calling split(" ") is different: it uses the exact space separator and can preserve empty pieces between consecutive spaces. The choice should follow the contract.

The worked example standardizes whitespace by splitting into words and joining those words with one space. For "  calm   sea  ", split() produces ["calm", "sea"], and " ".join(words) produces "calm sea". All-whitespace input produces an empty word list and therefore an empty string. join is called on the separator string, which is inserted between pieces rather than at the beginning or end.

Slices support other transformations. text[::-1] reverses the sequence, while text[:3] takes up to the first three characters. A comprehension can transform selected characters before joining them, for example "".join([ch for ch in text if ch != "-"]). A plain loop may be clearer for more involved state or conditions. Repeatedly appending to a list of pieces and joining once is often a clearer construction pattern than repeatedly concatenating a growing string.

Common pitfalls include forgetting that methods return new values, removing spaces when they should be preserved, and assuming every user-perceived symbol occupies one Python character. Unicode combining marks and emoji sequences can make visual text more complex than basic indexing suggests. These exercises specify simple text rules so behavior stays precise. Test empty text, leading and trailing whitespace, repeated separators, mixed case, and punctuation. Never introduce normalization simply because it looks attractive: changing case or discarding punctuation is a decision the problem must authorize.

problems.title: Normalize whitespace
problems.prompt: Implement solve(text). text is a string. Treat any whitespace recognized by Python str.split() as a separator, remove leading and trailing whitespace, and replace each internal whitespace run with one ordinary space. Preserve all non-whitespace characters exactly.
problems.python:
def solve(text):
    return " ".join(text.split())
problems.explanation: Calling split with no explicit separator turns the input into a list of non-whitespace pieces. It treats repeated whitespace as a single separating region and produces no empty pieces for leading or trailing whitespace. Joining those pieces with one ordinary space then creates exactly the requested normalized output. The separator appears only between pieces, so there is no need for a separate strip operation after joining. Empty text and all-whitespace text both split into an empty list, whose join result is the empty string. Case, punctuation, and all other non-whitespace characters remain unchanged because the pipeline only separates and reconnects pieces. Using split(" ") would have different behavior for repeated spaces and tabs, so the omitted argument is intentional.
problems.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary/output space for n input characters.
hints: Break the text into whitespace-separated pieces.
split() without an argument handles runs and multiple whitespace kinds.
Join the resulting pieces with " ".

quiz.question: How does text.split() differ from text.split(" ")?
choices: The no-argument form handles whitespace runs and omits empty pieces
The explicit-space form handles all whitespace kinds
quiz.explanation: The default splitting rule treats runs of whitespace as separators without producing empty edge pieces.

problems.title: Alphanumeric mirror check
problems.prompt: Implement solve(text). text contains only ASCII characters. Keep ASCII letters and digits, compare letters case-insensitively, and ignore everything else. Return whether the resulting sequence is a palindrome. An empty resulting sequence is a palindrome.
problems.explanation: First construct the exact sequence the contract says to compare. Visit each character, keep it when it is alphanumeric, and lowercase it before adding it to the list of retained characters. Because the input is restricted to ASCII, isalnum matches the intended letters and digits without introducing broader Unicode-category questions. Join the retained characters into one string, then compare it with its reversed slice. A palindrome reads identically in both directions, so equality supplies the Boolean answer directly. Empty and punctuation-only inputs produce an empty cleaned string; reversing it gives the same empty string, which correctly returns True. Normalization is justified here by the explicit problem rules, unlike tasks that require preserving the original text exactly.
problems.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for n input characters.
hints: Build the sequence that should actually be compared.
Keep alphanumeric characters and lowercase letters.
Compare the cleaned string with cleaned[::-1].

quiz.question: Why does punctuation-only input return True?
choices: Cleaning leaves an empty sequence, equal to its reverse
The implementation skips testing such input
True is the default for every string
quiz.explanation: The contract defines the empty cleaned sequence as a palindrome, and the equality check naturally handles it.

title: Reason about time and space
summary: Count growing work and memory instead of measuring one lucky run.
objectives: Distinguish worst-case time from a single measurement
Count total iterations in nested and sequential loops
Separate auxiliary storage from output space
lesson:
Big O describes how resource use grows with input size. It does not predict exact milliseconds. If a loop inspects n items once, doubling n roughly doubles its work: O(n). A pair of loops that each run n times performs n squared pairs: O(n²). Constants and lower-order terms disappear from the growth class, so 3n + 20 is O(n). State what n means; a grid may need two dimensions, rows r and columns c.

The useful mental model is a budget of primitive operations. Add costs for consecutive phases, but multiply genuinely independent repeated work. A nested loop is not automatically quadratic. In the example below, the inner loop runs i times, producing 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) operations. That triangular sum is n(n - 1)/2, still O(n²). By contrast, two pointers that only move forward across one array may perform O(n) total steps despite nesting.

Space requires its own account. A running total and a few indices occupy O(1) auxiliary space. Copying the input costs O(n); building a returned list of length n has O(n) output space. Python slicing allocates a new list, and membership in a list scans potentially every element. Hiding those operations inside a loop does not make them free. Hash-table lookup is usually discussed as expected O(1), not an unconditional worst-case guarantee.

For n = 4, the example checks six pairs: none for index zero, then one, two, and three. It does not inspect sixteen pairs, but both counts grow quadratically. Interview analysis should name the dominant operation, count its repetitions, and mention early exits separately from worst-case behavior. Avoid claiming an algorithm is fast simply because a small sample finishes instantly.

Practice deliberately: before typing, write the meaning of every variable and the condition that must remain true after each iteration. Trace the worked example on paper, including the state immediately before termination. Then test empty input, one element, repeated values, and a case where no result exists whenever the contract permits them. A passing example is evidence, not a proof. Explain why every valid candidate is considered and why discarded candidates cannot improve the answer. Finally, separate auxiliary memory from the returned output when stating space complexity, and count how often each input element is visited rather than guessing from indentation alone.

problems.title: Count larger successors
problems.prompt: Implement solve(nums) returning the number of index pairs (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] < nums[j]. nums is a list of at most 200 integers. Use explicit pair enumeration for this first exercise. Do not modify nums.
problems.explanation: Choose the earlier index first, then enumerate only later indices. This ensures every permitted pair appears exactly once and excludes both self-pairs and reversed duplicates. For [2, 1, 3], the pairs have values (2, 1), (2, 3), and (1, 3); the latter two satisfy the strict comparison. Equality must not count. The outer loop has n iterations, but the inner lengths are n - 1, n - 2, down to zero, so the number of comparisons is n(n - 1)/2. Only count and two indices are stored. The empty list and a singleton naturally return zero without requiring special branches. This deliberate brute-force solution is also a useful oracle for validating a future faster algorithm on small random inputs.
problems.complexity: O(n²) time; O(1) auxiliary space
hints: Fix the earlier index first
Start the second index at i + 1
Count only strict increases

quiz.question: How many candidate pairs are visited for n elements?
quiz.explanation: Each unordered pair of distinct indices is visited once.

problems.title: Running peak totals
problems.prompt: Implement solve(nums) returning a list whose entry i is the maximum of nums[0:i+1]. nums is a possibly empty list of integers. Do not modify it. Solve in one pass without repeatedly slicing or calling max on prefixes.
problems.explanation: The state peak summarizes all values seen so far. Before the first item there is no peak, represented by None rather than zero so negative inputs work. For every new value, either that value raises the peak or the old peak remains correct. Append the updated peak because the output describes the prefix including the current element. In the example the state changes from absent to 3, stays 3, rises to 5, then stays 5. Inductively, if peak was the maximum of the preceding prefix, comparing it with one new value produces the next prefix maximum. This visits each value once and avoids rescanning growing prefixes. The returned list occupies linear space, while the additional running state is constant.
problems.complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space excluding O(n) output
hints: Track one maximum instead of each prefix
Do not initialize the maximum to zero
Append after updating the maximum

quiz.question: Why is repeated max(nums[:i+1]) slower?
choices: The prefixes are rescanned and copied
quiz.explanation: The growing scans and slices sum to quadratic work.

title: Linear search and binary boundaries
summary: Use ordering to safely discard half of a search range.
objectives: Choose linear search when ordering is absent
Maintain a half-open binary-search invariant
Handle duplicates with a lower-bound search
lesson:
Search asks where a target belongs or whether it exists. With no useful structure, linear search is the reliable baseline: examine elements until you find a match or exhaust the list. It takes O(n) worst-case time and works on unsorted inputs. Binary search gains its speed from sorted order. A failed comparison can eliminate an entire region only because every element there is known to be too small or too large.

Use a half-open candidate interval [lo, hi). Initialize lo = 0 and hi = len(nums). For lower bound, seek the first position whose value is at least target. The invariant is that every index before lo is too small, while every index at or after hi is large enough. The unexplored middle lies between. When nums[mid] < target, set lo = mid + 1; otherwise set hi = mid. Each update strictly shrinks the interval. When lo equals hi, that shared position is the boundary, possibly len(nums).

Trace nums = [1, 3, 3, 8] and target = 3. Start with [0, 4), choose mid = 2, and move hi to 2. Now mid = 1 again has a large-enough value, so hi becomes 1. The last comparison at mid = 0 moves lo to 1. The answer is 1, the first duplicate, rather than an arbitrary matching position.

Never read nums[lo] after termination without checking lo < len(nums). An empty array has a valid insertion position but no element. Common bugs mix inclusive and exclusive conventions, leave mid inside the next range, or silently assume an unsorted array is searchable. Sorting first can cost more than one linear search and can destroy original indices. The example deliberately returns an insertion position; existence is a separate check.

title: Binary search on the answer
summary: Turn optimization into a monotone yes-or-no question.
objectives: Build a monotone feasibility predicate

lesson:
Binary search does not require an array. It requires an ordered domain and a condition that changes only once. Many optimization problems ask for the smallest capacity, speed, or limit that makes a plan possible. Replace “find the best answer” with “would this candidate be enough?” If enough remains true for every larger candidate, the answers have the shape false, false, true, true. Search for the first true value.

The example asks for the smallest positive integer processing speed that finishes separate jobs within a time budget. A job of size x takes ceil(x / speed) units, computed exactly as (x + speed - 1) // speed. The jobs cannot share a partially used unit. Larger speeds never increase total time, so feasibility is monotone. Under the stated assumption that the budget is at least the number of positive jobs, max(jobs) is feasible; speed one is the smallest candidate.

For jobs [3, 7] and budget 4, speed four needs one plus two units, so it works. Speed two needs two plus four, so it fails. Speed three needs one plus three and works, making it the smallest feasible speed. Keep a closed numerical interval [lo, hi] containing the answer. On success set hi = mid; on failure set lo = mid + 1. Termination leaves one candidate.

A feasibility function must model the real rules. Rounding the combined job size instead of rounding each job separately would incorrectly allow jobs to share time. Also prove the initial upper bound is feasible; if the task can be impossible, define how that is reported. If one predicate evaluation scans n jobs and the numerical range has width R, total time is O(n log R), not merely O(log R). Floating-point ceiling is unnecessary and can lose precision for large integers.

title: Two pointers with a shared invariant
summary: Move two boundaries without reconsidering discarded candidates.
objectives: Use opposite-end pointers on sorted data
Use read/write pointers for compaction
Explain why each pointer move is safe
lesson:
Two pointers is a family of techniques rather than one recipe. Two indices describe a region or divide processed from unprocessed data. The speedup comes from moving each index in only one direction, so work is proportional to total movement instead of the number of possible pairs. The important question is not where to place the pointers but what their positions mean.

For a sorted pair-sum search, begin at opposite ends. If the current sum is smaller than the target, the left value cannot pair successfully with any available right value because the current right value is already the largest. Discard that left value. If the sum is too large, discard the right value symmetrically. With [1, 2, 4, 7] and target 6, first compare 1 + 7, move right leftward, compare 1 + 4, then move left rightward. The pair 2 + 4 succeeds. Every eliminated row or column of possible pairs is justified by sorted order.

Read/write pointers solve a different problem: filtering or compressing a sequence. The read pointer inspects each input value; the write pointer marks the next output position. For sorted duplicate removal, the prefix before write contains exactly the distinct values seen so far. Only copy a value when it differs from the last kept value. The unread suffix must remain intact, so write never gets ahead of read.

Beware of applying opposite-end sum logic to an unsorted list. Sorting can be allowed, but it costs O(n log n) and changes index meaning. Also make mutation explicit: an in-place prefix length is a different contract from returning a new array. Pointer equality matters because many pair problems require two distinct indices. The example below returns values, so it does not promise original positions or every possible pair.

title: Fixed and variable sliding windows
summary: Update neighboring ranges by adding and removing their boundaries.
objectives: Maintain a fixed-length rolling aggregate
Shrink a variable window to restore validity
Recognize when negative values break sum monotonicity
lesson:
A sliding window represents a contiguous range. Moving its boundaries lets neighboring ranges share work. Instead of recalculating a length-k sum from scratch, add the new rightmost value and subtract the departing leftmost value. After initialization, each fixed-window move takes constant time. This works even with negative values because the window length, not a sum condition, controls movement.

Variable windows use a validity condition. For the longest substring with no repeated characters, keep character counts inside [left, right]. Add the next character; if it repeats, remove characters from the left until uniqueness returns. Record the length only after restoring validity. Both boundaries only move forward, so a nested shrinking loop still removes each character at most once. That amortized reasoning is more useful than simply counting nested indentation.

Trace “abca”. The valid window grows through “a”, “ab”, and “abc”. Adding the final “a” duplicates one character. Remove the original “a”, producing “bca”, which is valid again and still has length three. Removing just one arbitrary occurrence or clearing the entire map would discard information unnecessarily. The map must describe exactly the current window, and the best answer records history beyond that current state.

Sum-based variable windows often require nonnegative numbers. If values are positive, extending a window cannot decrease its sum and removing from the left cannot increase it. Negative values break that monotonicity, so the standard minimum-length target-sum routine may miss valid ranges. Check this assumption before borrowing a pattern. Also distinguish longest valid from shortest sufficient windows: they update the answer at different moments. Empty windows, zero counts, and off-by-one lengths are common errors. A window including both endpoints has length right - left + 1, whereas a half-open window uses right - left.
