problems.title: Best fixed-size sum
problems.prompt: Implement solve(nums, k) returning the maximum sum of a contiguous window of exactly k integers. The contract guarantees 1 <= k <= len(nums). Values may be negative. Use a rolling sum.
problems.python:
def solve(nums, k):
    current = sum(nums[:k])
    best = current
    for right in range(k, len(nums)):
        current += nums[right] - nums[right - k]
        best = max(best, current)
    return best
problems.explanation: Initialize the sum of the first k elements and also use it as the initial best. Starting best at zero would be wrong when every legal window has a negative sum. Each later step advances the window exactly one position: add nums[right] and subtract nums[right - k], the element that just left. The invariant is that current equals the sum of the window ending at right. For the example, the length-two windows have sums one, three, and four, so the answer is four. All legal windows appear once, including the initial one. This implementation uses a temporary slice of length k for initialization, so its auxiliary space is O(k); a manual initial loop could reduce it to O(1) without changing the main idea.
problems.complexity: O(n) time; O(k) auxiliary space for the initial slice

title: Prefix sums and range differences
summary: Pay once to answer many range questions quickly.
objectives: Build a prefix array with a leading zero
Convert inclusive ranges to prefix differences

lesson:
A prefix sum records the total before a position. Define prefix[0] = 0 and prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]. Then the sum of the half-open range [left, right) is prefix[right] - prefix[left]. The leading zero makes ranges beginning at index zero follow exactly the same formula. Preprocessing takes O(n) time and storage; every later sum query takes O(1).

For nums = [4, -1, 3, 2], the prefix array is [0, 4, 3, 6, 8]. The inclusive range from index one through three is prefix[4] - prefix[1] = 8 - 4 = 4. Draw the prefixes as two overlapping stretches from the beginning: subtraction cancels the shared stretch and leaves only the requested segment. Clearly state whether a query’s right endpoint is inclusive; mixing conventions is the usual source of wrong answers.

Prefix sums also transform a subarray search into a lookup. If the current prefix is p and a subarray must sum to target, its earlier prefix must equal p - target. Keep frequencies of prefixes already seen. Add that frequency to the answer, then record the current prefix. The initial prefix zero has frequency one so a valid subarray beginning at index zero is counted. Querying before recording prevents an empty subarray from being counted when target is zero.

Unlike positive-only sliding windows, the prefix-frequency technique works with negative numbers because it uses an algebraic identity rather than monotonicity. Repeated prefix values matter: each occurrence represents a different starting boundary. A set would lose that multiplicity. Static prefix arrays are less suitable for frequent edits, since changing one element changes every later prefix. The example focuses on static queries; later data structures can trade more complex updates for faster changing-range workloads.

title: Hash maps for counting and grouping
summary: Design keys that summarize exactly what makes items equivalent.
objectives: Use dictionaries for frequencies and first-seen state
Choose immutable canonical grouping keys
Preserve the output order required by a contract
lesson:
A hash map associates keys with values. In Python, dictionaries support expected constant-time lookup, insertion, and update, making them useful for remembering facts about previously processed items. A set records presence; a dictionary can additionally record frequency, first position, accumulated totals, or a whole group. Pick the stored value to match the question rather than collecting information you never use.

For counting, the pattern counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1 handles both new and repeated values. Suppose the input is [“red”, “blue”, “red”]. After each step, the dictionary is {red: 1}, then {red: 1, blue: 1}, then {red: 2, blue: 1}. If the task asks for the first unique item, counting alone is insufficient to express the order of selection: perform a second scan of the original input and return the first item with count one.

Grouping requires a canonical key: two items should share a key exactly when they belong together. Anagrams of lowercase words have equal counts for all twenty-six letters. A tuple of those counts is immutable and hashable, unlike a list. Sorting each word is another valid key, but adds a length-dependent sorting cost. Empty strings share the all-zero signature and therefore form a legitimate group.

Python dictionaries preserve insertion order. If you append items to groups as they arrive, members retain their input order; iterating the dictionary returns groups in first-seen-key order. Do not assume all languages provide the same ordering guarantee, and do not sort unless the contract requests it. Hash collisions do not make unequal keys identical: dictionaries also compare keys for equality. Complexity claims should say expected time for hashing and account for key construction. A twenty-six-entry signature is constant-sized only because this task fixes the alphabet.

title: Sorting keys, ties, and stable order
summary: Specify the complete ordering before writing a key function.
objectives: Build lexicographic tuple keys
Use stability to preserve meaningful tie order
Account for sorting time and temporary storage
lesson:
Sorting turns an unordered collection into a structure that supports scanning, grouping, and searching. Python’s sorted returns a new list; list.sort changes the list in place. Both are stable: items with equal keys retain their original relative order. Stability is a semantic guarantee, not an accident, and it often supplies the correct tie-break without adding an artificial field.

A key function transforms each item into the value used for ordering. Tuple keys are compared lexicographically: compare the first field, then the second only when the first ties, and continue as needed. To order scores descending but names ascending, use (-score, name). Setting reverse=True on the whole tuple would reverse both fields and produce the wrong name order. Write the contract in plain language first, including every tie-break, then translate it one field at a time.

Consider records [[“Mia”, 8], [“Ari”, 9], [“Bo”, 8], [“Mia”, 8]]. Sorting by (-score, name) places Ari first, then Bo, then the two Mia records in their original order. If the task instead requires arrival order among equal scores, use only -score. Adding name would violate the contract even though the result looks tidy.

Custom comparators are occasionally needed when a relation cannot be expressed conveniently as a key. In Python, functools.cmp_to_key adapts a comparator, but a key is usually easier to reason about and is computed once per item. Any comparison rule must be consistent and transitive; contradictory pairwise decisions cannot define a reliable sorted order. Do not use subtraction as a universal comparator for strings or structured objects. Standard sorting costs O(n log n) worst-case time, with Python’s implementation able to exploit existing runs. Returning a sorted copy also requires linear storage for the new list.

title: Intervals and merging
summary: Sort by start time, then keep one active interval.
objectives: State endpoint semantics explicitly
Merge overlapping ranges with a running frontier
Use finish-time order for maximum compatible selections
lesson:
An interval compresses many positions into two boundaries. Before solving an interval problem, decide whether endpoints are included and whether touching intervals overlap. Closed ranges [1, 3] and [3, 5] share the point three and therefore overlap. Half-open meeting ranges [1, 3) and [3, 5) do not overlap and can be scheduled consecutively. This one distinction changes a comparison operator and can change the entire answer.

To merge closed intervals, sort by starting position. Keep the last merged interval as the active frontier. If the next start is at most the active end, the intervals overlap, so extend the end to the maximum of both ends. Otherwise, the active interval is finished and the next one begins a new output group. Sorting guarantees that no later interval can reach back across a genuine gap.

For [[1, 4], [2, 3], [4, 7], [9, 10]], begin with [1, 4]. The contained interval [2, 3] changes nothing; taking its end directly would incorrectly shrink the frontier. The touching interval [4, 7] extends the frontier to seven. Finally, nine is beyond seven, so append [9, 10]. The result is [[1, 7], [9, 10]]. Copy endpoints into output records rather than mutating inner lists supplied by the caller.

Not every interval task uses start order. Selecting the largest number of nonoverlapping meetings uses increasing finish time: the earliest finishing available meeting leaves the most room for the future. This greedy choice needs a different proof from merging. Do not transfer one sorting key to every interval problem. Also distinguish counting the union’s length, returning merged ranges, and counting removable meetings; they may share preprocessing but ask for different results. Empty input and fully nested ranges are especially useful tests for the merge invariant.

Practice deliberately: before typing, write the meaning of every variable and the condition that must remain true after each iteration. Trace the worked example on paper, including the state immediately before termination. Then test empty input, one element, repeated values, and a case where no result exists whenever the contract permits them. A passing example is evidence, not a proof. Explain why every valid candidate is considered and why discarded candidates cannot improve the answer. Finally, separate auxiliary memory from the returned output when stating space complexity, and count how often each input element is visited rather than guessing from indentation alone.

problems.title: Merge closed ranges
problems.prompt: Implement solve(intervals) returning sorted, merged closed integer intervals. Each input is [start, end] with start <= end. Overlapping or endpoint-touching ranges must merge. Do not mutate input or its inner lists.
problems.explanation: Sorting by start makes every newly examined interval the leftmost remaining one. The output contains completed disjoint intervals followed by one active interval that may still grow. When the next start is within that active interval, merge by taking the maximum end, which handles both extension and complete containment. If the next start is larger, there is a real gap and no future interval can bridge it from the left, so begin a new output interval. Equality merges because the ranges are closed and share that endpoint. Construct fresh [start, end] lists before changing endpoints, preventing accidental mutation of caller-owned inner arrays. In the example, the first three sorted intervals combine into [1, 7], while [9, 10] remains separate. Sorting dominates the linear merge scan.
problems.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) auxiliary sorting space and O(n) output
hints: Sort by start
Use max when extending an end
Closed endpoints merge on <=

choices: A contained interval must not shrink the frontier

problems.title: Keep the most meetings

problems.explanation: Sort meetings by increasing finish time, then accept each meeting that starts at or after the end of the last accepted one. The earliest-finishing feasible meeting leaves at least as much room for future meetings as any alternative first choice. Replacing another first choice with it cannot reduce the number of meetings that follow, giving the greedy exchange argument. Repeat the same reasoning for the remaining time. In the example, [1, 3], [3, 5], and [5, 7] form an optimal chain of three. Equality is allowed because intervals are half-open. Using None for the initially absent end avoids assuming all times are nonnegative. Selecting by shortest duration or earliest start lacks the same guarantee. Sorting costs O(n log n); the selection pass uses constant state beyond the sorted copy.
problems.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) auxiliary space for sorted copy

Accept start >= last_end
Think about replacing the first choice in an optimal schedule

quiz.explanation: Finishing earliest leaves a superset of the future time available after a later finish.

title: Stacks for nesting and parsing
summary: Resolve the most recent unfinished item first.
objectives: Model last-in-first-out dependencies
Validate nested delimiters with matching types
Evaluate postfix expressions with correct operand order
lesson:
A stack is a last-in-first-out collection. Python lists provide append to push and pop to remove the most recent item, both efficient at the end of the list. A stack fits tasks where the most recently opened obligation must be completed first: nested brackets, undo history, recursive calls, and expressions whose operands arrive before their operator.

Bracket validation illustrates the mental model. An opening bracket creates an unfinished obligation, so push it. A closing bracket must match the top obligation. If the stack is empty or the types differ, the input is invalid immediately. After processing all symbols, the stack must be empty: leftover openings are unmatched even if no closing mismatch occurred. For “([])”, push “(”, push “[”, match and pop “[”, then match and pop “(”. For “([)]”, the first closing parenthesis fails because the latest opening is a square bracket.

Postfix notation removes parentheses by placing each operator after its operands. Read tokens left to right. Push numbers. For an operator, pop the right operand first and the left operand second, compute left operator right, and push the result. In “8 3 - 2 *”, subtraction produces five, then multiplication produces ten. Reversing the two popped operands would silently work for addition while breaking subtraction.

Separate parsing rules from the data structure. A minus sign inside “-4” belongs to a numeric token, whereas a standalone “-” is an operator. Define which characters may be ignored in bracket input and which operators a calculator supports. Avoid eval: it solves a different parsing problem and executes arbitrary Python. A valid postfix expression must never require more operands than are available and should leave exactly one final result. Each token is pushed or consumed a constant number of times, giving linear processing time, while nesting depth or unfinished operands determine peak stack space.

Practice deliberately: before typing, write the meaning of every variable and the condition that must remain true after each iteration. Trace the worked example on paper, including the state immediately before termination. Then test empty input, one element, repeated values, and a case where no result exists whenever the contract permits them. A passing example is evidence, not a proof. Explain why every valid candidate is considered and why discarded candidates cannot improve the answer. Finally, separate auxiliary memory from the returned output when stating space complexity, and count how often each input element is visited rather than guessing from indentation alone.

problems.title: Check mixed delimiters
problems.prompt: Implement solve(text) returning whether (), [], and {} delimiters are properly nested and balanced. Ignore all other characters. Empty text is valid.
problems.explanation: The stack holds unmatched opening delimiters in their encounter order. Its top is the only opening that the next closing delimiter is allowed to complete. Push opening characters, ignore ordinary text, and for a closing character check both that an opening exists and that its type matches. The short-circuit condition prevents popping an empty stack. In the example, the square brackets finish before the parenthesis group, and both finish before the outer brace. A crossed structure such as ([)] is rejected even though its total counts balance. After the scan, a nonempty stack indicates openings that never closed, so the final answer depends on emptiness. Every delimiter is pushed and popped at most once, producing linear time and space proportional to maximum unmatched nesting depth.
problems.complexity: O(n) time; O(n) worst-case auxiliary space
hints: Store openings, not just a count
A closing delimiter must match the stack top
Check for leftover openings at the end

quiz.question: Why is counting each bracket type insufficient?
quiz.explanation: Crossed brackets can have balanced counts but invalid nesting.

problems.title: Evaluate postfix arithmetic
problems.prompt: Implement solve(tokens) evaluating a valid postfix expression of signed integer strings and operators +, -, *. Return its integer result. tokens is nonempty and guaranteed to describe exactly one valid expression. Do not use eval.
problems.explanation: Numbers become completed subexpression values on the stack. Each operator combines the two most recently completed values into one larger subexpression. Because the right operand was encountered later, it is popped first; the next popped value is the left operand. This order is crucial for subtraction. The example pushes eight and three, replaces them with five after subtraction, then pushes two and multiplies to obtain ten. A token such as -4 is parsed as an integer because only the exact token - means subtraction. The validity guarantee allows the implementation to assume enough operands and exactly one final value, simplifying error handling without changing the algorithm. Each token performs constant stack operations. As usual for introductory integer analysis, arithmetic costs are treated as constant; very large arbitrary-precision integers add digit-dependent costs.
problems.complexity: O(t) time and O(t) auxiliary space under unit-cost arithmetic, t = token count
hints: Push integer tokens
Pop right before left
Replace two operands with one result

quiz.explanation: The first popped value is the right operand, so compute 2 - 5.

title: Monotonic stacks and unresolved questions
summary: Keep only candidates that a future value can resolve.
objectives: Maintain a monotonic stack of indices
Distinguish strict from non-strict comparisons
Prove linear work through push/pop accounting
lesson:
A monotonic stack maintains values in increasing or decreasing order while tracking unresolved positions. It is useful for next-greater elements, previous-smaller elements, spans, and histogram boundaries. The stack is not the final answer; it stores questions waiting for a future element. Usually store indices so both values and distances remain available.

For the next strictly greater value to the right, scan left to right while keeping indices whose values are nonincreasing from bottom to top. When a new value exceeds the top value, it answers that top index’s question. Pop it and record the new value or distance, then continue because one arrival may resolve several older positions. Finally push the current index as a new unresolved question. Equal values stay on the stack when the requirement is strictly greater.

Trace [3, 1, 2, 4]. Index zero waits at value three. Index one waits above it at value one. Value two resolves index one but cannot resolve index zero, so index two is pushed. Value four then resolves index two and index zero. The last index has no greater value later and keeps the chosen sentinel. Every popped position receives its first qualifying future value: earlier scanned values did not qualify, and the current one is the first that does.

The inner while loop can pop many entries in one step, but each index is pushed once and popped at most once overall. That gives O(n) total stack operations, an amortized argument. Do not claim O(n²) solely because loops are nested. Comparison strictness is a common bug: replacing < with <= changes whether equal values resolve each other. Also avoid storing only values when the answer needs distances or original positions. A previous-greater span problem uses a related invariant but asks about the surviving blocker to the left rather than writing answers for popped future questions.

Practice deliberately: before typing, write the meaning of every variable and the condition that must remain true after each iteration. Trace the worked example on paper, including the state immediately before termination. Then test empty input, one element, repeated values, and a case where no result exists whenever the contract permits them. A passing example is evidence, not a proof. problems.title: Wait for a higher reading
problems.prompt: Implement solve(readings) returning, for each index, the distance to the next strictly higher reading on its right, or 0 if none exists. readings is a possibly empty list of integers.
problems.explanation: Store indices whose next higher reading has not been found. Their values are nonincreasing through the stack, so when a new value exceeds the top, that top’s answer is now known. Pop it and write the difference between the current index and its index. Repeat until the new value no longer exceeds the top, then push the current index. For [3, 1, 2, 4], the final four resolves the earlier two and three, while two already resolved one. Equal readings are deliberately not popped because the question asks for strictly higher values. Positions left on the stack never see a qualifying reading and retain zero. Each position is pushed once and popped at most once, so the nested loop still performs linear total work.
problems.complexity: O(n) time; O(n) auxiliary stack space and O(n) output
hints: Store unresolved indices
Pop only on strictly higher values
Distance is current index minus popped index

quiz.question: Can equal readings resolve one another here?
quiz.explanation: Equality does not satisfy strictly higher.

problems.title: Consecutive price span
problems.prompt: Implement solve(prices) returning for each day the number of consecutive days ending that day whose prices are all <= that day’s price. Count the current day. prices may be empty and contains integers.

Remove stack entries whose price is less than or equal to the current price; they cannot block the current span, and the current day supersedes them as a blocker for future smaller prices. After removing them, the top is the nearest surviving greater price, so subtract its index from the current index. If no blocker remains, every day from zero through the current day qualifies, yielding index + 1. In the example, price 75 spans [60, 70, 60, 75], length four. Equality is removed here, unlike next-strictly-greater resolution, because equal prices belong inside the span. Each index participates in at most one push and one pop.

No blocker means span index + 1

To make the result strictly decreasing

title: Queues, deques, and breadth-first search
summary: Process discoveries in arrival order to reveal distance layers.
objectives: Use deque for efficient first-in-first-out removal
Mark nodes when enqueuing to avoid duplicates
Compute shortest paths in unweighted graphs
lesson:
A queue processes items first in, first out. This matches work that should be handled in arrival order. Python’s collections.deque supports append on the right and popleft on the left efficiently. A list’s pop(0) shifts the remaining elements, so repeating it can turn otherwise linear processing into quadratic work. A deque also supports both ends, making it useful for window algorithms later.

Breadth-first search uses a queue to explore an unweighted graph in distance layers. Start by assigning the source distance zero and enqueuing it. Remove a node, inspect its neighbors, and enqueue each undiscovered neighbor with distance one larger. Nodes at distance one enter before distance two, and so on. Therefore the first discovery of a node gives its shortest number of edges from the source.

Consider edges 0–1, 0–2, 1–3, and 2–3. After processing zero, the queue contains one and two with distance one. Processing one discovers three at distance two. When two later sees three, it must not enqueue it again. Mark discovery when enqueuing, not when removing, so multiple parents cannot create duplicate pending work. The resulting distances are [0, 1, 1, 2].

For a grid, cells are graph nodes and allowed moves define edges. Bounds checks and obstacle tests replace an explicit adjacency list. State whether a path length counts edges or visited cells: a source already at the destination has zero moves but one visited cell. Breadth-first search guarantees shortest paths only when every move has equal cost; weighted edges need different algorithms. In adjacency-list graphs, each node is enqueued at most once and each edge is inspected a constant number of times, giving O(V + E) time. Unreachable nodes keep a sentinel such as -1. Empty input, disconnected components, self-loops, and blocked destinations clarify the contract and expose queue mistakes.

Practice deliberately: before typing, write the meaning of every variable and the condition that must remain true after each iteration. Trace the worked example on paper, including the state immediately before termination. Then test empty input, one element, repeated values, and a case where no result exists whenever the contract permits them. A passing example is evidence, not a proof. Finally, separate auxiliary memory from the returned output when stating space complexity, and count how often each input element is visited rather than guessing from indentation alone.

problems.title: Unweighted reach distances
problems.prompt: Implement solve(graph, source) returning shortest directed-edge distances from source to all vertices, or -1 for unreachable vertices. graph is a nonempty adjacency-list array of valid vertex indices; source is valid. Cycles, repeated edges, and self-loops are allowed.
problems.explanation: Initialize every vertex as unreachable, then set the source distance to zero before enqueuing it. The queue processes nodes in nondecreasing distance order. When an unseen neighbor is discovered from a node at distance d, assign d + 1 immediately and enqueue it once. Any shorter path would have come from an earlier layer already processed, so this first assignment is optimal. In the example, vertices one and two have distance one, vertex three has distance two, and isolated vertex four remains -1. Assigning distance before enqueueing also handles repeated edges, self-loops, and cycles without duplicate work. The graph is directed, so follow only listed outgoing edges. deque avoids the shifting cost of removing the front of a Python list, keeping traversal linear in vertices plus listed edges.
problems.complexity: O(V + E) time; O(V) auxiliary space including distance and queue
hints: Use distance -1 as the unseen marker
Mark before appending
Follow only the listed directed edges

quiz.question: When should a vertex be marked discovered?
quiz.explanation: Early marking prevents several parents from placing the same vertex in the queue.

problems.title: Shortest grid route
problems.prompt: Implement solve(grid) returning the fewest orthogonal moves from top-left to bottom-right, or -1 if impossible. grid is a nonempty rectangular matrix with 0=open and 1=blocked. A blocked start or end is impossible. Do not modify grid; a one-cell open grid returns 0.

Breadth-first search explores all positions reachable in one move before those requiring two, so the first time the destination is removed from the queue its stored distance is minimal. Reject blocked endpoints before starting. Store visited coordinates separately to preserve the grid, and mark each neighbor before enqueueing it to avoid repeated discoveries through different routes. The example admits a four-move path across the top-left open corridor and down to the destination. A one-cell open grid returns zero because the starting position already satisfies the goal. If the queue empties first, no allowed route exists. Each cell is enqueued at most once and checks only four neighbors, bounding time and memory by the number of cells.

title: Follow links without losing your place
summary: Model nodes as separate objects and traverse a chain safely.
objectives: Build and traverse a singly linked list
Distinguish a node reference from its stored value
Use a sentinel to simplify deletion
lesson:
A Python list is an indexed sequence, but a linked list is a chain of separate node objects. Each node stores a value and a reference called next. That reference identifies the next node; it is not an integer position. The final node points to None. The head variable identifies the first node, and head is None for an empty chain. Imagine a treasure hunt where each card contains both a prize and the location of the next card.

Traversal begins with current = head. While current is not None, inspect current.value and then move to current.next. Before every iteration, current is the first unprocessed node. This invariant gives both correctness and termination for an acyclic chain: each step consumes one node and never returns to it. Do not move head unless you intentionally want to change the list's entry point. A separate current reference lets you inspect everything while retaining access to the beginning.

For the chain 7 → 2 → 9, an accumulator starts at zero. Visiting 7 makes it seven; following next visits 2 and makes it nine; visiting 9 makes it eighteen. Following the final next gives None, so the loop stops. Accessing current.value after that point would fail. Equal values do not mean equal nodes: two cards can both contain 7 while occupying different places in the chain.

Deletion changes a link rather than shifting all later values. To remove a node after previous, assign previous.next = previous.next.next. Removing the head looks different unless you add a temporary sentinel node before it. With a sentinel, every real node has a predecessor, and the returned head is sentinel.next. After deletion, keep the predecessor in place so consecutive matching nodes are checked.

These exercises accept ordinary arrays as transport data and build nodes inside solve. That representation keeps inputs readable without changing the pointer reasoning. Building the chain costs linear time and space; traversing it uses constant auxiliary state. Practice drawing three nodes and naming each reference before translating the arrows into assignments.
python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next_node=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next_node

head = Node(7, Node(2, Node(9)))
current = head
total = 0
while current is not None:
    total += current.value
    current = current.next
print(total)  # 18

title: Reverse arrows in a controlled order
summary: Save the untouched suffix before changing any link.
objectives: Maintain processed and unprocessed regions
Reverse an entire linked list iteratively
Reconnect a reversed interval using a sentinel
lesson:
Reversing a linked list means changing the direction of every next reference. It does not require swapping stored values, and it does not work by moving a cursor backward: a singly linked node has no previous link. The reliable mental model is two regions. previous identifies an already reversed prefix, and current identifies the untouched suffix. Initially previous is None and current is the original head.

Each iteration must perform three conceptual actions in order. Save the remaining suffix with following = current.next. Redirect the current arrow with current.next = previous. Finally advance the region boundaries: previous = current and current = following. The saved reference is essential. If you overwrite current.next first and then follow it, you travel into the reversed prefix and lose your route to the unprocessed nodes.

Trace 1 → 2 → 3. After processing 1, the reversed prefix is 1 → None and current is 2. After processing 2, the prefix is 2 → 1 → None and current is 3. The final step produces 3 → 2 → 1 → None. When current becomes None, previous is the new head. Returning the old head would expose only the new final node.

Reversing a subrange adds reconnection work. Locate the node immediately before the interval, remembering that the interval may begin at the head. A sentinel makes this predecessor available in all cases. The first node in the interval will become its tail. Repeatedly detach the node after that tail and insert it immediately after the predecessor. For positions two through four in 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5, move 3 before 2, then move 4 before 3. The result is 1 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 5.

Pointer bugs often create a cycle or silently discard a suffix. Draw each temporary reference before modifying arrows, and test empty, singleton, and whole-list intervals. On already built nodes, full reversal takes linear time and constant auxiliary space. Our array-based interface also charges for building and serializing nodes. Those interface costs do not change the constant-space nature of the pointer transformation itself.
python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next_node=None):
        self.value, self.next = value, next_node

head = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3)))
previous, current = None, head
while current is not None:
    following = current.next
    current.next = previous
    previous, current = current, following
head = previous
result = []
while head is not None:
    result.append(head.value)
    head = head.next
print(result)  # [3, 2, 1]

title: Make two pointers share the work
summary: Use speed and distance invariants to find middles and cycle entries.
objectives: Choose an explicit even-length middle convention

lesson:
Two pointers are useful when their relative positions reveal information that one pointer cannot obtain immediately. In a singly linked list, slow can move one link per iteration while fast moves two. This creates a speed invariant rather than an index lookup. On an acyclic chain, when fast reaches the end, slow has covered approximately half the distance. Checking fast and fast.next before taking two steps avoids dereferencing None.

For the chain 10 → 20 → 30 → 40, both pointers start at 10. After one iteration slow is 20 and fast is 30. After the next, slow is 30 and fast is None. This convention selects the second middle for an even number of nodes. If an interview asks for the first middle, initialization or the stopping rule must change. State the convention rather than treating one answer as universally correct.

The same speeds detect cycles. Once both pointers are inside a cycle of length c, fast gains one position per iteration relative to slow. Their relative distance is considered modulo c, so they must eventually occupy the identical node. Compare object identity, not values: different nodes can store equal integers. An acyclic chain instead causes fast to reach None.

Finding the cycle entry takes a second phase. After a meeting, reset one pointer to head while leaving the other at the meeting node. Move both one link at a time. If the entry is a links from head and the meeting is b links beyond the entry, the first phase implies a + b is a multiple of c. Therefore walking a more steps from the meeting reaches the entry, exactly when the pointer from head arrives there.

Never serialize a cycle using an unbounded traversal. Return the entry index by stopping at the identified entry object. title: Understand the call stack and base cases
summary: Give each call a smaller task and a precise return meaning.
objectives: Define a recursive function’s contract
Identify a decreasing measure and base case
Account for call-stack space
lesson:
Recursion is a function solving a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of that problem. The most useful mental model is a stack of unfinished requests. Each call has its own parameters and local variables. When a call reaches a base case, it returns a value to the caller waiting directly above it. A recursive function must define what it returns, when it can answer immediately, and how its recursive calls move toward that stopping point.

Consider summing values beginning at index i. Define total(i) to mean the sum of values[i] through the final element. If i equals len(values), there are no elements left, so the answer is zero. Otherwise the answer is values[i] + total(i + 1). For [4, 1, 6], calls descend through indices zero, one, two, and three. The last returns zero; the suspended calls then return six, seven, and eleven. The additions happen while the stack unwinds.

Do not replace this reasoning with the slogan that recursion is a loop. A loop stores state explicitly, while recursion can preserve unfinished work in many stack frames. In the summation example, there are n + 1 calls and at most n + 1 active frames. The time is linear and the auxiliary stack space is linear. Python does not generally eliminate tail calls, so even a recursive function whose final action is another call still consumes stack space.

A decreasing measure proves termination. For the sum, len(values) - i decreases each time. For a nested list, each call handles a proper child of the current container; a finite, acyclic input eventually reaches integers or empty lists. Check your base cases before indexing or destructuring. An empty input should have an explicit meaning rather than accidentally throwing an exception.

Recursion is particularly expressive for trees and nested data because the input already has recursive structure. It is not always the best implementation for a long flat list. These exercises intentionally bound depth to keep the Python call stack safe. Practice writing the return contract in plain language, tracing three calls, and counting total work independently from maximum active depth.

title: Generate subsets and permutations
summary: Build a decision tree and undo each temporary choice.
objectives: Distinguish subsets from ordered arrangements
Copy completed paths before saving them
Prevent repeated values from producing duplicate results
lesson:
Backtracking explores a decision tree by making a temporary choice, exploring everything beneath it, and undoing that choice before trying another branch. A path list represents the partial answer. The call stack remembers which alternatives are still available. This approach is useful when the requested output is a collection of combinations or arrangements rather than one numeric result.

For subsets of [2, 5], each element has two decisions: include it or exclude it. One traversal yields [], [5], [2], and [2, 5]. An equivalent start-index approach records the current path as a valid subset, then chooses each later element as the next member. The increasing index ensures an element is used at most once and that [2, 5] is generated without also generating [5, 2]. Subsets ignore order; permutations preserve order and therefore require a different availability rule.

For permutations of [2, 5, 7], the first position has three options, the second has two remaining options, and the third has one. A used array marks which input positions already appear in the current path. When path reaches the required length, save path.copy(). Appending path itself would store a reference to the same mutable object; later pop operations would change previously saved results as well.

Repeated values complicate generation. Sorting places equal candidates beside each other. For unique permutations, skip an unused candidate when its equal predecessor has not been used in the current path. That rule chooses equal values in a consistent relative order while still allowing multiple copies to appear in one complete permutation. For subsets, an analogous skip applies only to duplicate siblings at the same recursion level.

Always undo exactly the state you changed: append pairs with pop, and used[index] = True pairs with resetting it to False. A return taken too early can prevent cleanup and corrupt sibling branches. Enumeration also has unavoidable output cost. There are 2^n subsets and n! permutations when all values differ, and copying each answer costs up to n. An efficient generator still becomes expensive quickly. Bound input sizes and specify result ordering so tests compare answers consistently.

def subsets(values):
    result, path = [], []
    def visit(start):
        result.append(path.copy())
        for index in range(start, len(values)):
            path.append(values[index])
            visit(index + 1)
            path.pop()
    visit(0)
    return result

print(subsets([2, 5]))  # [[], [2], [2, 5], [5]]

title: Prune constrained searches safely
summary: Reject impossible branches without discarding valid solutions.
objectives: Write validity checks before recursion
Distinguish sound pruning from a heuristic
Restore state after successful and failed searches
lesson:
A constrained search explores only choices that can still lead to a valid answer. Backtracking provides the search structure, and pruning removes branches that are already impossible. The important word is impossible. A rule that merely looks promising can discard a real solution. To justify pruning, explain why no completion of the current partial path could satisfy the requirements.

Suppose positive candidate values are sorted and we are building combinations with a target sum. Track remaining, the amount still needed. A candidate greater than remaining cannot work, and neither can any larger candidate, so the loop may stop. Positivity matters: if negative values were allowed, a later negative candidate could repair an overshoot. If a candidate may be reused, recurse with the same index; if it may be used once, recurse with the next index. That one argument encodes a major difference in the problem contract.

Searching for a word on a grid adds spatial constraints. A state includes a row, a column, the position in the word, and the cells already used by the current path. Reject an out-of-bounds cell, a character mismatch, or a repeated cell. After accepting a cell, explore its up, down, left, and right neighbors. A visited set belongs to the current path, not to the entire search: a cell unavailable in one attempt may be necessary in another.

For a grid containing rows AB and CD, the word ABD follows the top-left, top-right, and bottom-right cells. ABA cannot reuse the starting cell, even though neighboring characters appear suitable. This illustrates why matching letters alone is insufficient; the path history changes which next choices are legal.

Undo temporary state when returning from a branch, including successful branches if the input or state will be reused. A copied path is appropriate when collecting answers; a boolean early return is appropriate when only existence matters. Grid word search can still take exponential time because many prefixes may match. Constraints and pruning reduce explored branches but do not magically make exhaustive search polynomial. Use small, explicit input limits, include impossible cases, and test that a failed first attempt does not poison later starting positions.

def combinations(candidates, target):
    candidates = sorted(candidates)
    result, path = [], []
    def visit(start, remaining):
        if remaining == 0:
            result.append(path.copy())
            return
        for index in range(start, len(candidates)):
            value = candidates[index]
            if value > remaining:
                break
            path.append(value)
            visit(index, remaining - value)
            path.pop()
    visit(0, target)
    return result

title: Visit trees in a meaningful order
summary: Choose a traversal based on when a node’s information is needed.
objectives: Read compact level-order tree encodings
Compare depth-first and breadth-first traversal
Preserve level boundaries in a queue
lesson:
A binary tree node contains a value and up to two child references, left and right. Unlike a linked list, a traversal can branch. A leaf has no children, and an empty tree has no root. The useful mental model is a hierarchy of smaller trees: the left child is the root of one subtree, and the right child is the root of another. This recursive structure makes both recursive and explicit-stack algorithms natural.

Depth-first traversal follows a branch before returning to alternatives. Preorder processes the current node, then the left subtree, then the right. Inorder processes left, current, right. Postorder processes both children before current. These names specify when the current node is handled relative to its descendants. Postorder is useful when a parent needs results from children, while preorder is useful when information flows downward.

Breadth-first traversal uses a queue to visit nodes by distance from the root. Enqueue the root, repeatedly remove the oldest node, and enqueue its existing children. To return separate levels, capture the queue length at the start of each outer iteration and remove exactly that many nodes. Newly enqueued children belong to the next level and must not change the current loop’s count.

For a root 8 with children 3 and 10, where 3 has right child 6, breadth-first levels are [8], [3, 10], and [6]. The compact input encoding is [8, 3, 10, null, 6]. Read the root first, then consume left and right entries for each non-null node waiting in a queue. Null marks a missing child and does not receive child slots of its own. This is different from treating positions as a complete-tree array with index formulas.

An empty queue or None child is a stopping condition, not a real node with a special value. Zero and negative values are legitimate data. Avoid list.pop(0), which shifts remaining elements; collections.deque supports efficient removal from the left. Every real node enters and leaves the queue once, giving linear traversal time. Auxiliary queue size follows the tree’s maximum width, which can be much larger than its height. State whether your space bound includes the built input tree and returned output.

title: Use global BST bounds
summary: A search-tree rule constrains every descendant, not just each child.
objectives: Validate strict binary-search-tree ordering

lesson:
A binary search tree adds an ordering invariant to an ordinary binary tree. In the strict convention used here, every value in a node’s left subtree is smaller than that node’s value, and every value in its right subtree is larger. Duplicate values are therefore invalid. Other applications choose a duplicate-placement policy, but an algorithm must follow one explicit convention throughout.

The word every is crucial. Checking only a parent and its immediate children is insufficient. Consider a root 10, a left child 5, and a right child 12 beneath that 5. The local edge 5 → 12 looks valid because 12 is larger than 5, but 12 still lies inside the root’s left subtree and violates the requirement to be smaller than 10. Validation must retain constraints inherited from all ancestors.

A recursive validator can pass an open interval, lower < value < upper. The root initially has no finite bounds. Moving left replaces the upper bound with the current value; moving right replaces the lower bound. Keep the other bound unchanged because it represents an ancestor constraint. For the misplaced 12, the inherited upper bound remains 10 and exposes the problem immediately. None children are valid empty subtrees.

Inorder traversal offers another viewpoint. Visiting left, node, right produces strictly increasing values in a valid strict BST. This can support validation or order-statistic tasks, but it should not tempt you to assume the tree is already valid when the task is to check it. Bounds are especially clear when explaining exactly which ancestor restriction failed.

Once validity is guaranteed, ordering can avoid work. To sum values in an inclusive interval [low, high], ignore the left subtree when the current value is below low; every value there is even smaller. Ignore the right subtree when the current value is above high. Values on a boundary still count. A balanced tree may make a narrow query fast, but an arbitrary BST can be a chain, so worst-case time remains linear. Never claim logarithmic performance merely because a structure is called a BST; height depends on its shape and balancing policy.

title: Combine depths and locate shared ancestors
summary: Return one useful summary from each subtree while tracking a larger answer.
objectives: Separate node depth from edge-count path length
Compute a tree diameter using child heights
Find an LCA and handle missing targets
lesson:
Many tree problems become simpler when each recursive call returns a compact summary of its subtree. Height is a classic example: define an empty subtree’s height as zero and a leaf’s height as one. A nonempty node then has height one plus the larger child height. This definition counts nodes on a downward path. A path length reported in edges uses a different convention, so state units before writing a formula.

The diameter is the maximum number of edges on any simple path between two nodes. At a particular node, the longest path passing through it uses the deepest left branch and the deepest right branch. If child heights count nodes, their sum already counts the edges in that through-node path. A leaf has child heights zero and zero, producing diameter zero. Return one plus the maximum child height upward, while updating a separate best diameter with the sum. Returning the diameter itself would not give the parent the downward height it needs.

A lowest common ancestor, or LCA, is the deepest node that is an ancestor of both targets; a node counts as its own ancestor. In a general binary tree, values do not imply search direction. Search both subtrees. If one target is found on each side, the current node joins the paths and is their LCA. If only one side returns a candidate, propagate it upward. Finding the current node as a target can stop that branch when target existence is guaranteed.

Missing targets require additional care. A basic LCA routine may return the one target that exists even though the other is absent. Our exercise explicitly checks membership before running the LCA search and uses unique values to identify targets unambiguously. When both targets are the same value, that existing node is the answer.

For a root 1 with children 2 and 3, where 2 has children 4 and 5, the diameter is three edges and the LCA of 4 and 5 is 2. Sketching this small example exposes both units and branching. Postorder computations visit each node once. Stack space follows height, and a skewed tree can make that height linear rather than logarithmic.

title: Keep the best candidates with heapq
summary: Maintain a small frontier instead of sorting everything.
objectives: Explain the min-heap invariant
Maintain a bounded heap for top-k selection
Encode deterministic tie-breaking in heap entries
lesson:
A heap is a partially ordered collection designed to expose one extreme efficiently. Python’s heapq module implements a min-heap in an ordinary list. The smallest entry is at index zero, and each parent is no greater than its children. The whole list is not sorted. Reading other positions as if they were ranked results is a common mistake; repeated heappop operations are needed to extract ascending order.

heappush adds an entry and restores the invariant in logarithmic time. heappop removes the minimum with the same cost. heapify turns an existing list into a heap in linear time. A tuple entry is compared lexicographically, so its first field is the primary priority and later fields break ties. Include a deterministic tie-breaker before an object that cannot be compared, or equal priorities may cause a TypeError.

To retain the k largest numbers seen so far, use a min-heap of at most k entries. Its root is the weakest retained candidate. Until the heap is full, push each number. Afterward replace the root only when a new number is larger. For [6, 2, 9, 4] and k = 2, the heap first retains 2 and 6, then replaces 2 with 9, and ignores 4. The remaining values are 6 and 9; the root 6 is the second largest.

This works because discarded numbers are no better than the weakest of k retained numbers. Later input can only improve that threshold. Duplicates count as separate observations unless the problem explicitly asks for distinct values. A request for top-k frequencies adds another layer: count each value first, then rank distinct keys by their counts and a specified tie-breaker.

A bounded heap usually costs O(n log k) time, useful when k is much smaller than n. Sorting the final retained heap costs O(k log k) if ranked output is required. Be precise about invalid ranks and k = 0, since inspecting heap[0] on an empty heap fails. For tiny or one-shot inputs, sorting may be simpler; choose a heap when repeated updates or limited retained state are central to the task.

title: Merge sorted streams with a frontier
summary: Keep one candidate per source and advance only the winning source.
objectives: Maintain one heap entry per nonempty stream
Explain why the smallest frontier value is globally next
Stop a merge early for rank queries
lesson:
When several sources are individually sorted, their order can be exploited without sorting all values again. Picture each source as a line of customers already ordered by ticket number. Only the front customer from each line can be the next overall customer. A min-heap stores that frontier: one currently available item from every nonempty source.

Each heap entry can be a tuple of value, source index, and position within that source. The value decides which item comes next. Source index and position make ties deterministic and tell the algorithm where to find the replacement. Pop the smallest entry, append its value to the answer, and push the next item from the same source if one exists. Other sources do not advance because their front items have not yet been consumed.

For streams [1, 7], [2, 3], and [1, 5], the initial frontier contains 1 from source zero, 2 from source one, and 1 from source two. Popping the first 1 exposes 7 from its source. Popping the other 1 exposes 5. The next minimum is 2, which exposes 3. Continuing yields [1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7]. Equal values remain separate observations unless the contract explicitly requests deduplication.

The key invariant is that every unconsumed source contributes its smallest remaining item. Any hidden item in that source is no smaller than its frontier item. Therefore the minimum across frontier items is also the minimum across all unconsumed items. This proof is the reason the algorithm works; it would fail if even one source were unsorted.

A rank query can stop after k pops instead of materializing the entire merged sequence. Validate the rank first, then count removals. The heap never needs more entries than the number of nonempty sources, giving O(log s) work per pop or push for s sources. Empty sources are simply absent from the initial frontier. Avoid physically removing each source’s first array element, which would shift its contents. Store an index instead, leaving inputs unchanged and allowing efficient sequential progress.

import heapq

streams = [[1, 7], [2, 3], [1, 5]]
heap = [(stream[0], source, 0)
        for source, stream in enumerate(streams) if stream]
heapq.heapify(heap)
merged = []
while heap:
    value, source, index = heapq.heappop(heap)
    merged.append(value)
    index += 1
    if index < len(streams[source]):
        heapq.heappush(heap, (streams[source][index], source, index))
print(merged)  # [1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7]

title: Index shared prefixes with a trie
summary: Store words as character paths and distinguish prefixes from complete words.
objectives: Build a trie from lowercase words
Track complete-word endings separately from child edges
Answer prefix counts and lexicographic suggestions
lesson:
A trie organizes strings by shared prefixes rather than by whole-word comparison. Each edge represents one character, and following edges from the root spells a prefix. Words such as car, cart, and cat share the c and a edges before branching. The root represents the empty prefix. A node is not automatically a complete word: the path ca exists, but ca may never have been inserted.

Store a terminal marker at nodes where complete words end. Then exact lookup succeeds only if every character edge exists and the final node is terminal. Prefix lookup needs only the path to exist. This distinction handles a word that is also a prefix of another word, such as car and cart. The marker belongs on the node, separate from the dictionary of character children, so it cannot collide with a legitimate character.

To count distinct words beginning with a prefix, maintain a count at the root and at every node visited during insertion. Deduplicate input words first or check whether a word is already terminal before incrementing counts. For words car, cart, and cat, the count after ca is three, while the count after car is two. Querying an absent edge returns zero immediately. The empty prefix reaches the root and matches all inserted words.

For autocomplete, first walk to the node for the requested prefix. Then perform a depth-first traversal below it, trying child characters in sorted order. Emit the current word before visiting longer descendants when the node is terminal. This produces lexicographic order because a word sorts before its own extensions. Stop after collecting the requested number of suggestions rather than exploring irrelevant later branches.

Trie performance is measured in characters, not just word count. Building takes time proportional to the total inserted characters, and a prefix count query takes time proportional to the prefix length. The structure can use substantial memory because each distinct prefix needs a node and child mapping. For a small static dictionary, sorting and binary search may be a reasonable alternative. Tries shine when shared-prefix operations are central. Test repeated input words, empty queries, missing prefixes, and words that end at internal nodes.

title: Graph representations and traversal
summary: Model relationships explicitly and choose traversal by the information needed.
objectives: Build adjacency lists from edge lists
Explain DFS and BFS invariants
Handle cycles and disconnected vertices
lesson:
A graph separates entities from relationships. Choose a vertex identifier and decide whether each relationship is directed before choosing an algorithm. An adjacency list stores outgoing neighbors; an undirected edge needs two entries. For sparse graphs this is usually more economical than an n-by-n matrix. A set of neighbors removes duplicates but changes iteration behavior and adds hashing overhead.

Depth-first search carries an unfinished path on a stack. It is useful for reachability and component discovery. Breadth-first search carries a frontier in a queue. In an unweighted graph, every newly discovered layer is one edge farther from the source, so first discovery proves the shortest edge distance. This claim does not extend to arbitrary weighted edges.

Trace a triangle with an isolated fourth vertex. Without a visited marker, the triangle can generate endless work; without an outer loop, the isolated vertex is never considered in a component count. Mark on discovery, not after removal from the worklist. Prefer collections.deque for FIFO removal, and an explicit stack when a recursive chain could exceed Python's call-stack limit.

Practice workflow
Start with the stated contract, not a memorized implementation. Write down the input size, legal values, expected return type, and behavior for empty or disconnected cases. Construct a tiny example with at least one choice between alternatives. Trace the working example on paper, recording the structure that carries state after each step. Ask what fact makes it safe to discard an alternative or commit an update; that fact is the correctness argument.

Next, implement the first exercise without looking at the reference. Use the hints one at a time: each should reduce uncertainty rather than replace your reasoning. Compare your output with the supplied cases, then invent a case that targets your own most fragile assumption. Passing examples provides evidence, not a proof. Explain why every valid input is covered by the invariant and why the algorithm terminates.

Finally, review the second exercise under its suggested time budget. Spend the opening minutes choosing a representation and the closing minutes checking boundaries and complexity. Count work across the whole execution rather than just the visible loop nesting. Include auxiliary structures and recursion depth in space analysis. After checking the reference, rewrite one sentence explaining the mistake you were most likely to make. Revisit that sentence before the next lesson.

The queue holds discovered vertices in nondecreasing distance order. problems.title: Earliest exact pair

problems.title: Best fixed-width diversity
problems.prompt: Implement solve(values, width). values is a list of integers and width is an integer. If width < 1 or width > len(values), return -1. Otherwise return the earliest starting index of a length-width contiguous window containing the greatest number of distinct values.
problems.explanation:
The map stores frequencies only for the current fixed-width window. Adding the incoming value and removing the outgoing value updates it in constant expected time. Delete zero-frequency keys so the map size equals the distinct count. Score only complete windows; earlier prefixes are not legal candidates. Updating the best result only on a strict improvement preserves the earliest start when scores tie. A set alone cannot safely remove a value that still has another occurrence inside the window.

Before coding, name what each variable represents and state the invariant that should remain true after one iteration. Trace the first sample by hand, then deliberately try the smallest allowed input and an input containing repeated values. These checks expose different failure modes: initialization, update order, and accidental assumptions about uniqueness. The reference implementation returns its result rather than printing it, so a test runner can compare values directly. Keep the contract separate from implementation choices: another correct solution may use different intermediate structures, but must preserve the specified ordering, boundary behavior, and return type.
problems.complexity: Expected time O(n); auxiliary space O(width).
